topics.title: AI & Agent Legibility
topics.fullTitle: AI & agent legibility, explainability, auditability, governance UX

methods.method: Over-reliance / under-reliance rate on a seeded-error task set
methods.measures: Give participants tasks where the AI is deliberately WRONG on a known subset. Over-reliance = fraction of AI-wrong tasks where the human matched the AI anyway; under-reliance = fraction of AI-correct tasks where the human overrode it. This is the canonical HCI operationalization and directly quantifies whether your legibility/explanation design moved reliance in the right direction.

methods.method: RAIR / RSR (Relative AI Reliance & Relative Self-Reliance)
methods.measures: Separates the two directions of appropriate reliance: RAIR = did the user switch TO the AI when the AI was right? RSR = did the user stick to themselves when the AI was wrong? Lets you prove a design improved good reliance without just trading one failure for the other.

methods.method: Behavioral (not self-reported) trust via agreement/switch fraction
methods.measures: Agreement fraction, switch fraction, and follow-high-confidence fraction measured from logs. Because self-reported trust surveys diverge from actual reliance behavior, you instrument what users DO (did they open the trace, did they override, did they click the citation) rather than what they say.

methods.method: Confidence calibration curve / reliability diagram
methods.measures: Plot stated confidence vs. empirical accuracy in bins. A well-calibrated signal sits on the diagonal; LLM verbalized confidence bows above it (overconfident). Use this to decide whether a confidence display is safe to ship or is actively misleading users.

methods.method: Citation-attribution audit
methods.measures: Sample generated claims, open each cited source, and score whether the source actually supports the claim (not just whether the URL resolves). Produces a misattribution rate (the metric that exposed Perplexity's ~37%). Distinguishes 'checkable' from 'correct.'

methods.method: FPR / FNR on a real overeager-action test set + red-team exfiltration set
methods.measures: For any gating/guardrail: false-positive rate (benign actions wrongly blocked = friction) and false-negative rate (dangerous actions let through = residual risk) on (a) real traffic, (b) curated real dangerous actions, (c) synthetic adversarial attempts. This is exactly how Anthropic evaluated auto mode (n=10,000 real, n=52 overeager, n=1,000 exfiltration).

methods.method: Approval-fatigue instrumentation
methods.measures: Track blanket-approval rate, time-on-prompt, and approval rate vs. prompt sequence position. A rising approval rate / falling dwell time as prompts accumulate proves the human-in-the-loop has decayed into rubber-stamping (Anthropic's 93% is the benchmark to beat).

methods.method: Audit replay / reconstruction test
methods.measures: Take a completed agent session and ask an outsider (or auditor persona) to reconstruct WHY each side effect happened using only the stored record. If they can't tie action -> input -> policy -> identity, your auditability is nominal. This is a governance-grade usability test, not a lab task.

methods.method: Wizard-of-Oz for autonomy level and escalation thresholds
methods.measures: Before building the agent, fake it with a human backend to test where users WANT approval gates vs. silent execution, and what escalation copy earns trust. Cheaply finds the right autonomy-per-action-class map (which actions are worth an interruption) without engineering the whole pipeline.

tactics: Spend the user's attention budget deliberately: silently auto-run the reversible mass of actions and reserve interruption for the few irreversible/high-blast-radius ones. Every needless confirmation you cut makes the ones that remain get read. This is the anti-approval-fatigue move.

Classify every agent action by reversibility and blast radius, then map an oversight mode to each class (silent / notify-after / approve-before / escalate-to-human). Ship this map as an explicit artifact; it's the spine of a governance-first design and a great teardown lens.

Make the summary-to-payload binding a hard design rule: whatever human-readable line you show at the approval moment must be rendered from the exact bytes/inputs being committed, never from a parallel description. Adopt WYSIWYS from crypto for agent tool calls.

Prefer simulation over explanation for high-stakes writes: a dry-run diff ('1,240 rows will change, here are 5') earns more calibrated trust than any prose rationale, and it can't be faithfully faked the way a reasoning trace can.

Design the audit record as a product surface, not a log: each entry ties action -> resolved input -> policy version -> actor identity -> data lineage, tamper-evident, reconstructable long after the session. This is what compliance/risk buyers actually pay for and what stops the 'trust us' objection.

Turn confidence into a forcing function, not a badge: instead of '92%', use uncertainty to trigger a checkable action ('I'm unsure here, verify against X') or to withhold the answer until the user commits a provisional judgment. Uncertainty framed to provoke System-2 thinking reduces over-reliance; a number just gets normalized.

Give provenance teeth: attach the specific supporting span to each claim and make one-click verification effortless, so the checkable-vs-correct gap becomes the user's cheap habit rather than a leap of faith.

Kill anthropomorphic reassurance in high-stakes flows: replace 'Don't worry, I've handled it' with evidence the user can inspect. Confident tone widens the calibration gap; legible artifacts close it. This is the trust-vs-trustworthiness belief-shift.

Make the guardrail reasoning-blind: any automated second check should judge the proposed action from user-intent + the action alone, not the agent's self-narration, so a confused or injected agent can't rationalize its way past its own reviewer.

Position zero-retention / session-scoping as a legibility feature, not just a legal checkbox: show the user what is and isn't persisted, when context is flushed, and log metadata-only. Visible data boundaries are a trust signal for the 'Sam' buyer who fears their prompts becoming training data or leaking.

resources.title: Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance
resources.source: John D. Lee & Katrina A. See, Human Factors (2004)
resources.why: The canonical source for calibrated trust, resolution, and appropriate reliance. Every serious HCI-AI trust paper cites it. Read this to sound like you understand trust at the mechanism level, not the vibes level.

resources.title: Humans and Automation: Use, Misuse, Disuse, Abuse
resources.source: Raja Parasuraman & Victor Riley, Human Factors (1997)
resources.why: Gives you the four-word vocabulary (use/misuse/disuse/abuse) that names every automation failure you'll find in a teardown. 3,000+ citations. Foundational and still the sharpest framing of over/under-trust.

resources.title: To Trust or to Think: Cognitive Forcing Functions Can Reduce Overreliance on AI in AI-Assisted Decision-Making
resources.source: Zana Buçinca, Maja Barbara Malaya, Krzysztof Z. Gajos (Harvard), ACM CSCW (2021)
resources.why: The study proving explanations alone don't fix over-reliance and can worsen it, and that cognitive forcing functions do. The empirical backbone for the whole 'your XAI panel is trust theater' argument. Gajos's lab is the one to follow.

resources.title: How we built Claude Code auto mode: a safer way to skip permissions
resources.why: A real production account of governance UX with hard numbers: 93% blanket-approval (approval fatigue), reasoning-blind two-stage classifier, FPR cut 8.5%->0.4%, 20+ irreversible-action block rules. The best single primary source on gating agent actions at scale.

resources.title: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (18 guidelines) + Microsoft HAX Toolkit
resources.source: Saleema Amershi et al., Microsoft Research, CHI (2019); HAX Toolkit
resources.why: The most-cited practitioner framework, structured by interaction phase (initially / during / on error / over time). The HAX Toolkit turns it into design patterns and a playbook you can apply directly in a teardown. Skip the fundamentals, mine the error-handling and 'scope services when in doubt' guidance.

resources.title: People + AI Guidebook (Explainability + Trust, Feedback + Control, Errors + Graceful Failure chapters)
resources.why: The most usable industry design reference for AI trust surfaces. The Explainability+Trust and Errors+Graceful-Failure chapters are the ones worth stealing patterns from; treat 'Determine if AI adds value' as your anti-abuse gut check.

resources.title: Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
resources.source: Miao Xiong et al., ICLR (2024), arXiv:2306.13063
resources.why: The evidence that verbalized LLM confidence is poorly calibrated and overconfident. Cite this to justify NOT shipping a raw confidence % badge, and to argue for self-consistency/ensemble-derived confidence instead.

resources.title: Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think (CoT faithfulness)
resources.why: The primary source for 'the reasoning trace is not the reason.' Essential to stop treating chain-of-thought as audit evidence. Pairs with the general finding that models act on hidden cues then rationalize.

resources.title: Ledger Clear Signing initiative + 'Transaction Verification: A Solution to Blind Signing'
resources.why: The crypto industry's canonical framing of WYSIWYS (What You See Is What You Sign) and blind-signing as the top exploited wallet vulnerability. Directly portable to agent tool-call approval. The best crypto-native source for the summary-to-payload binding principle.

resources.title: A Statistical / Decision-Theoretic Framework for Measuring AI Reliance
resources.source: Ziyang Guo, Yifan Wu, Jason Hartline, Jessica Hullman (Northwestern), 2024, arXiv:2401.15356
resources.why: Gives rigorous definitions of over/under-reliance and RAIR/RSR so your teardowns and studies measure reliance correctly instead of hand-waving. Hullman is a key voice on uncertainty visualization and reliance methodology worth following.

resources.title: Second-Hand Hallucinations: Investigating Perplexity's AI-Generated Sources
resources.why: The empirical basis for 'citations make claims checkable, not correct' and the ~37% misattribution figure. A ready-made teardown seed for AI-search provenance UX. Shows the link/attribution decoupling in a real product.

resources.title: Zero Data Retention in LLM-based Enterprise AI Assistants
resources.why: Covers the architecture and UX tradeoffs of zero-retention / session-scoping (context flushed on task completion, metadata-only logging, the multi-turn usability cost). The load-bearing reference for the compliance-UX / 'Sam fears his data leaks' angle.

teardownTargets.product: A crypto wallet's transaction-signing sheet (MetaMask / Rabby / Phantom approval + signing flow)
teardownTargets.why: The purest legibility-vs-blind-signing battleground: does the sheet decode calldata into human-readable fields (WYSIWYS), simulate the post-transaction state, flag unlimited approvals and drainer contracts, and is the displayed summary provably the thing being signed? Irreversible side effects make every legibility failure catastrophic. Rabby vs MetaMask is a strong compare-and-contrast.

teardownTargets.product: Perplexity's answer + citations UI (or ChatGPT Search / Google AI Overviews)
teardownTargets.why: Provenance-as-trust-signal done at scale with a measured ~37% misattribution rate. Tear down whether citations are spot-checkable (does clicking surface the exact supporting span?), whether the UI conflates citation count with reliability, and how it handles the checkable-vs-correct gap. Perfect 'invisible problem' + belief-shift material.

teardownTargets.product: A coding-agent approval flow (Cursor Agent / GitHub Copilot agent mode / Claude Code)
teardownTargets.why: The clearest propose-then-commit and approval-fatigue teardown. Does it gate before side effects? Which actions are allowlisted vs gated by reversibility/blast radius? Does it show a legible action timeline or a raw dump? Does confirmation fatigue set in? You can literally read the tool-call order, which is your signature edge.

teardownTargets.product: An enterprise AI copilot's audit / activity log (Microsoft 365 Copilot, Salesforce Agentforce, or a Glean/Writer-style assistant)
teardownTargets.why: Auditability-vs-observability in a product bought by compliance. Tear down whether the log ties action -> resolved input -> policy -> identity -> data lineage and is reconstructable, or whether it's just health telemetry and reasoning prose dressed as an audit trail. Governance-first, directly matches the 'Sam' enterprise buyer.

teardownTargets.product: An AI-assisted high-stakes decision UI (a fraud/AML review queue, a clinical decision-support tool, or a credit/lending copilot)
teardownTargets.why: Where over-reliance and confidence display do real damage. Tear down whether it uses cognitive forcing functions or just shows answer+explanation+confidence-badge, whether the confidence signal is calibrated, and whether escalation/human-in-the-loop gates the right actions. The strongest place to show calibrated-trust theory changing a concrete screen.

subNodes.label: Calibrated trust, not maximized trust (Lee & See)
subNodes.oneLiner: The design goal is matching perceived trustworthiness to actual trustworthiness, so reliance tracks reliability. Trust that's too high (over-reliance) and too low (under-reliance) are BOTH failures.
subNodes.body: Founder 'Sam' thinks the goal is to make users trust the AI more. Wrong. A crypto/AI product that inflates trust past its real capability manufactures the exact blow-up (a bad trade auto-signed, a hallucinated answer acted on) that destroys the brand. You design for the gap between real and perceived competence, not for a trust number going up.

subNodes.label: Misuse / Disuse / Abuse (Parasuraman & Riley, 1997)
subNodes.oneLiner: Automation fails three ways: misuse (over-trust the machine), disuse (ignore it after false alarms), abuse (deployer automates a task that shouldn't be automated without regard for the operator).
subNodes.body: A single vocabulary for every failure you'll find in a teardown. 'Users leak' is usually disuse (too many false-alarm confirmations trained them to click through) or the aftermath of misuse (one over-trusted action burned them). 'Abuse' names the founder's own sin: shipping autonomy the workflow can't safely absorb.

subNodes.label: Legibility = a readable event timeline, not a system-call dump
subNodes.oneLiner: An agent is legible when a non-engineer can reconstruct what it did and why from the UI alone. 'Researched 14 sources, found 3 schedule conflicts' is legible; 'calendar_conflict_check() returned array[3]' is not.
subNodes.body: Agentic AI/crypto products fail here constantly: they either hide the machinery entirely (opaque, untrustworthy) or expose raw traces (unreadable, so users tune out). Legibility is the translation layer between the two, and it's a pure design problem a code-reading designer is uniquely equipped to solve because you can see both the raw events and the human intent.

subNodes.label: Approve BEFORE side effects (propose-then-commit)
subNodes.oneLiner: Confirmation only counts if it gates the irreversible action. Anything shown after the write happened is incident documentation, not approval.
subNodes.body: This is the single most common code-visible lie in agent UIs: a 'confirm?' dialog that the code fires after the DB write / on-chain broadcast / email send already committed. Only a designer reading the call order catches it. In crypto (irreversible transfers) and enterprise write-actions, this is the difference between a control and a decoration.

subNodes.label: Explanation ≠ understanding; explanations can INCREASE over-reliance (Buçinca/Gajos)
subNodes.oneLiner: Adding an explanation often just makes users defer harder, because the presence of a rationale reads as competence regardless of the rationale's quality.
subNodes.body: Kills the reflexive 'add an explainability panel' fix. If the explanation doesn't force the user to engage (a cognitive forcing function), you've built trust theater that raises the over-reliance you were trying to cure. This is a belief-shift post in itself: 'Your XAI panel is making things worse.'

subNodes.label: The reasoning trace is not the reason (CoT unfaithfulness)
subNodes.oneLiner: A model's stated chain-of-thought is fluent post-hoc narration, not a faithful transcript of what drove the output; models change answers on hidden cues then rationalize.
subNodes.body: Directly attacks the 'show the agent's thinking = trustworthy' pattern that AI products lean on. A designer who understands this stops treating reasoning traces as audit evidence and starts treating them as UX affordance only. What you CAN audit are the tool calls and their inputs/outputs, not the prose.

subNodes.label: Verbalized confidence is decorative unless it's calibrated
subNodes.oneLiner: LLM self-reported confidence is systematically overconfident: answers claiming 80-100% confidence are correct far less than 80% of the time, so a raw confidence number misleads.
subNodes.body: Ends the lazy 'add a confidence % badge' pattern. If you surface an uncalibrated number you are actively lying to the user with a precise-looking signal. Either derive confidence from something measurable (retrieval agreement, ensemble/self-consistency) or express uncertainty in a way that provokes checking rather than deferring.

subNodes.label: Citations make claims checkable, not correct
subNodes.oneLiner: A source link proves a claim can be verified; it does not prove the claim matches the source. Perplexity cites real URLs with invented attributions ~37% of the time.
subNodes.body: The provenance UI (footnotes, 'sources' chips) is the most powerful trust signal in AI search and the most abused. Understanding that the link and the attribution are separate reliability questions lets you design for spot-checkability (surface the exact quoted span) instead of decorative citation count.

subNodes.label: Auditability ≠ observability
subNodes.oneLiner: Observability answers 'is the system healthy?' for engineers; auditability answers 'why did it decide this, under what data and policy?' for a regulator or a burned user months later.
subNodes.body: Enterprise AI/crypto buyers (compliance, risk) buy auditability; teams often ship observability and think they're done. The audit record must be tamper-evident, tie an action to an identity + policy version + data lineage, and be reconstructable long after the session. This is a governance-first differentiator, not a log dump.

subNodes.label: Approval fatigue: every extra confirmation degrades ALL confirmations
subNodes.oneLiner: The more prompts a user sees, the less they read each one. Anthropic measured a 93% blanket approval rate on Claude Code permission prompts.
subNodes.body: The core paradox of human-in-the-loop: naive HITL (confirm everything) trains the reflexive click-through that makes the human oversight worthless, which is functionally disuse. Good governance UX spends the user's attention budget only on the few irreversible/high-blast-radius actions and auto-handles the rest.

subNodes.label: Two-tier gating: allowlist the reversible, gate the irreversible
subNodes.oneLiner: Any agent that mixes low-stakes reads and high-stakes writes. Auto-run reversible/read-only actions silently; reserve explicit human approval for irreversible or high-blast-radius ones (delete history, send external data, on-chain transfer, prod deploy). Anthropic's default ships 20+ block rules grouped as destroy/exfiltrate, degrade-security-posture, and bypass-review.
subNodes.body: Example: Claude Code auto mode: allowlisted tools skip straight to execution; everything else hits a classifier. A crypto wallet should sign a small same-token swap silently but hard-gate an unlimited-approval to an unknown contract.

subNodes.label: Cognitive forcing function
subNodes.oneLiner: High-stakes decisions where over-reliance is the risk and you need the human to actually think, not rubber-stamp. Withhold the AI's answer until the user commits a preliminary judgment, or make them click to reveal the recommendation, or ask them to check on-demand.
subNodes.body: Example: Buçinca/Gajos 2021: forcing users to make a provisional decision before seeing the AI suggestion measurably reduced over-reliance (vs. showing the answer + explanation up front, which did not).

subNodes.label: Clear Signing / WYSIWYS (What You See Is What You Sign)
subNodes.oneLiner: Any irreversible commit where the human-readable summary and the actual payload can diverge: crypto signing, agent tool calls, bulk operations. Decode the raw payload into human-readable fields on a trusted surface and guarantee the displayed summary IS the thing being committed.
subNodes.body: Example: Ledger Clear Signing + wallet transaction simulators (Blockaid, GoPlus): show 'grants unlimited USDT access to 0xUnknown' instead of 'Approve'. Direct analog for agents: render the resolved SQL / the exact email recipients, not 'update records'.

subNodes.label: Transaction/action simulation (dry-run preview)
subNodes.oneLiner: Before any state-changing action whose real effect is hard to predict from the request. Execute against a sandbox/fork and show the diff of what WOULD change (balances after, rows affected, files touched).
subNodes.body: Example: Wallet simulators show post-transaction balances and flag drainer contracts before signing. Agent equivalent: 'this will modify 1,240 rows and cannot be undone' with the actual row preview.

subNodes.label: Structured action timeline / trace as first-class UI
subNodes.oneLiner: Any multi-step agent so the user can reconstruct and interrupt. Render each step as a meaningful event (verb + object + result), collapsible from summary to raw payload, with the point where a side effect occurred clearly marked.
subNodes.body: Example: Claude Code's streaming tool-call log; Perplexity's step list ('Searching', 'Reading', 'Comparing'). Progressive disclosure: human summary on top, raw call underneath for the auditor.

subNodes.label: Spot-checkable provenance (quote the span, not just the link)
subNodes.oneLiner: RAG / AI-search / any grounded answer. Attach each claim to the specific supporting passage so a user can verify attribution in one glance, not a full-article read.
subNodes.body: Example: Highlight the exact sentence in the source that supports the claim. Counters Perplexity's failure mode where the URL is real but the attribution is fabricated.

subNodes.label: Reasoning-blind independent monitor
subNodes.oneLiner: When you need a genuine second check on an agent's action rather than a self-report. A separate classifier/reviewer judges the proposed action seeing only the user's request + the tool call, NOT the agent's own reasoning or tool outputs (which may be compromised by injection).
subNodes.body: Example: Anthropic's transcript classifier (Sonnet 4.6) is reasoning-blind by design; two-stage (fast yes/no filter, then CoT only on flagged items) cut false-positive blocks from 8.5% to 0.4% while keeping the cheap first pass.

subNodes.label: Escalation / graceful handoff on low confidence or out-of-scope
subNodes.oneLiner: When the agent hits its competence boundary. Route to a human, ask a clarifying question, or degrade to a narrower safe action instead of confabulating. Pair with an audit entry recording why it escalated.
subNodes.body: Example: Human-in-the-loop (intervene before effect) vs human-on-the-loop (review after) as an explicit design choice per action class, per Microsoft HAX Guideline 'support efficient correction' and 'scope services when in doubt.'

subNodes.label: Post-hoc confirmation (approve after the write)
subNodes.oneLiner: The dialog fires after the irreversible side effect already committed, so it can only inform, never prevent. Looks like a control in the UI; is a decoration in the code. Only visible by reading call order. Catastrophic in crypto and enterprise write-paths.

subNodes.label: Explainability panel as trust theater
subNodes.oneLiner: An explanation that the user can passively read raises deference regardless of its quality (Buçinca/Gajos). You spent effort making over-reliance worse. If the explanation doesn't force engagement or expose a checkable fact, it's decoration.

subNodes.label: Raw uncalibrated confidence % badge
subNodes.oneLiner: LLM verbalized confidence is systematically overconfident; a crisp '92%' implies a precision the model doesn't have. Users read the number's format as reliability. You've dressed a guess as a measurement.

subNodes.label: Citation count as a trust proxy
subNodes.oneLiner: More footnotes read as more rigor, but ~37% of Perplexity citations misattribute claims to real sources. Citation presence is orthogonal to citation accuracy; the UI conflates them and manufactures false confidence.

subNodes.label: Reasoning trace presented as audit evidence
subNodes.oneLiner: CoT is unfaithful post-hoc narration, not a record of what drove the output. Treating 'the agent explained its thinking' as accountability means your audit trail is fiction. Audit the tool calls and data lineage, which are real; treat the prose as UX only.

subNodes.label: Confirm-everything human-in-the-loop
subNodes.oneLiner: Floods the user with prompts, trains the 93%-blanket-approve reflex, and the human oversight becomes rubber-stamping (functionally disuse). You've built the appearance of control while destroying its substance via approval fatigue.

subNodes.label: Anthropomorphic reassurance instead of legibility
subNodes.oneLiner: 'Don't worry, I've got this' / a friendly avatar inflates trust via false anthropomorphism cues rather than actual evidence, widening the calibration gap. Especially predatory in finance/crypto where the confident tone masks real risk.

subNodes.label: Observability logs sold as an audit trail
subNodes.oneLiner: Latency/health telemetry can't answer 'why did the AI decide this, under which policy and data?' months later for a regulator or a burned user. Missing identity binding, policy version, data lineage, and tamper-evidence. Compliance buyers see through it immediately.

subNodes.label: Blind signing / opaque bulk action
subNodes.oneLiner: Asking for approval of something the UI can't or won't decode ('Approve', 'Run 47 operations') is a blank check. The user's consent is uninformed, so the control is void, and it's the single most exploited wallet vulnerability.

subNodes.label: The confirm dialog fires AFTER the side effect in the code path. The U...
subNodes.oneLiner: The confirm dialog fires AFTER the side effect in the code path. The UI shows 'Are you sure?' but the network/DB/on-chain call already executed. Only visible by reading the call order, not the screen.

subNodes.label: The displayed action summary is generated from a DIFFERENT source than...
subNodes.oneLiner: The displayed action summary is generated from a DIFFERENT source than the executed payload, so they can silently diverge (the 'Approve 10 USDC' shows benign while the signed calldata is an unlimited drainer approval). A code-reader checks that the rendered summary is derived from the exact bytes being committed.

subNodes.label: The 'confidence' number is the model's raw verbalized self-estimate, n...
subNodes.oneLiner: The 'confidence' number is the model's raw verbalized self-estimate, not derived from retrieval agreement or self-consistency, so it's uncorrelated with correctness. Invisible unless you trace where the number comes from.

subNodes.label: Citations are attached by a post-processing step that maps claims to p...
subNodes.oneLiner: Citations are attached by a post-processing step that maps claims to plausible-looking URLs, not by grounding generation in retrieved text, so link and attribution are decoupled. You see this by inspecting whether the cited span actually contains the claim.

subNodes.label: The audit log records the natural-language summary or the reasoning tr...
subNodes.oneLiner: The audit log records the natural-language summary or the reasoning trace but NOT the resolved tool inputs (final SQL, exact recipients, calldata) plus policy version and actor identity, so it can't reconstruct the decision. The gap is invisible until an incident forces a replay.

subNodes.label: The independent 'checker' or guardrail is fed the agent's own reasonin...
subNodes.oneLiner: The independent 'checker' or guardrail is fed the agent's own reasoning/output, so a prompt-injected or overconfident agent can talk its reviewer into approving. A real second opinion must be reasoning-blind; most aren't.

subNodes.label: Retries silently re-issue a side-effecting call after a denial or time...
subNodes.oneLiner: Retries silently re-issue a side-effecting call after a denial or timeout, causing duplicate writes/transfers with no idempotency key. Visible only in the retry logic, never in the happy-path UI.

subNodes.label: Streaming reasoning is rendered token-by-token so it FEELS like transp...
subNodes.oneLiner: Streaming reasoning is rendered token-by-token so it FEELS like transparency, but nothing in that stream is durably logged or tied to the committed action, so there's no artifact to audit after the session ends.

subNodes.label: 'Zero retention' is claimed in marketing but the client-side context/h...
subNodes.oneLiner: 'Zero retention' is claimed in marketing but the client-side context/history persists the sensitive payload to reconstruct multi-turn state, or a proxy logs full prompt bodies rather than metadata-only, so the retention boundary is nominal. Visible by inspecting what actually gets written where.

topics.title: Systems & State Machines
topics.fullTitle: Systems thinking, state machines & explicit system states

methods.method: State-coverage audit (enumerate legal vs reachable states)
methods.measures: Coverage ratio = designed-and-implemented states / total legal states in the machine. Build the state table per key surface (rows = states, columns = designed? implemented? tested? has-recovery?), then count the gaps. Turns 'the app feels unfinished' into a countable defect list.

methods.method: Story-per-state + Chromatic visual regression
methods.measures: Whether every legal state actually renders correctly, as a CI gate. Each Storybook story is one state; Chromatic screenshots all of them against a baseline. Measures state-render coverage and catches the moment a new state (or a regressed one) diverges from design. This is the design-QA bridge for state coverage.

methods.method: Error-recovery rate (unassisted)
methods.measures: Of the sessions/tasks that hit an error state, the percentage where the user recovered and completed the task without help. Distinct from error rate (how often errors happen). Recoveries hide the biggest design problems: a task 'succeeded' but only barely. Instrument by logging error-state entries and subsequent task completion.

methods.method: Time-to-feedback and time-in-state instrumentation
methods.measures: Latency from user action to first visible state change (the feedback-loop delay), and the distribution of dwell time per state. Long tails in 'loading' or 'pending' with no exit reveal missing timeout edges; short-then-repeated actions reveal a feedback gap causing double-submits.

methods.method: Transition-log / event-sourcing replay
methods.measures: Whether the states users actually reached match the states you designed. Log every (fromState, event, toState) transition; then diff the observed transition graph against the intended statechart. Unexpected edges = undesigned states shipping in production.

methods.method: Fault-injection / chaos on the client (throttle, offline, 500s, reorg)
methods.measures: How the UI behaves in the states you can't reproduce on a fast dev machine. Use Chrome DevTools network throttling/offline, mock 4xx/5xx/timeout, and for crypto simulate dropped/replaced transactions. Measures how many failure states have real designs vs default/blank rendering.

methods.method: Reducer/store code diff against mockups
methods.measures: The design-implementation state gap directly. List every case in the reducer / every discriminant in the union type, then map each to a mockup. Unmapped cases are states shipping without design. This is the code-reading designer's signature technique, and it produces the sharpest teardown evidence.

methods.method: Truthfulness audit (optimistic vs confirmed labeling)
methods.measures: For every optimistically-rendered value, whether the UI distinguishes 'shown but not confirmed' from 'confirmed'. Trace each optimistic write to whether there's a confirmed/finalized state and a rollback path. Measures how much of the displayed state is a promise vs a fact, the core trust question in crypto.

tactics: Lead the teardown with the state table, not the screenshot. Reconstruct the target's state machine from its behavior + code, then show the missing/undesigned states as a coverage matrix. This is the 'I read the code before I judge the design' proof and it's un-arguable in a way subjective critique isn't.

Reframe 'user leak' as 'unhandled state exits'. Map where users drop off to which state they were in (long loading, silent error, ambiguous empty). Founders hear 'churn'; you show them 'these three states have no recovery edge' and hand them a fix list.

For crypto/agent clients, sell finality honesty as a trust feature, not a limitation. The move is: optimistic where reversible, truthful where not, and make the distinction visible (pending vs confirmed vs finalized). Position it as 'never lie to the user about their money/their agent', which is exactly what earns Sam's trust.

Turn every spinner in the product into a question: 'what's the timeout branch?' Auditing loading states for their exit edges is fast, high-signal, and almost always finds dead ends. It's a repeatable teardown lens.

Ship the statechart as the shared artifact between you and their engineers. An XState/Stately diagram is readable by both design and code, so it eliminates the design-impl drift at the source and makes you the person who closed the gap, not just flagged it.

Instrument error-recovery rate before proposing redesigns, so you can prove impact. 'We took unassisted recovery from 40% to 78% on the failed-swap flow' is the kind of measurable outcome that converts a teardown into a retainer.

Use fault injection in demos. Throttle the network live and show the target product's dead spinner vs your designed loading/stale/error states. Making the invisible failure visible in real time is more persuasive than any deck.

Write the belief-shift post as 'your UI is a state machine you never drew', then show the boolean-soup-to-union refactor with a real product's inferred states. It's advanced, code-literate, contrarian to the Dribbble happy-path culture, and directly aimed at the founder audience.

resources.title: Stop using isLoading booleans
resources.why: The clearest short argument for status enums / state machines over boolean flags, with the concrete refactor. Load-bearing for the 'impossible states' mental model and directly readable by the engineers you'll work with.

resources.title: Make Impossible States Impossible
resources.why: Names the principle and traces it to Khourshid's finite-automata framing. The phrase itself is a useful belief-shift hook for a post.

resources.title: Infinitely Better UIs with Finite Automata (React Rally 2017)
resources.why: The origin talk: most UI code is already a state machine developers didn't formalize. Foundational, and the seed of XState. Watch for the AJAX-request-becomes-tangled demo.

resources.title: XState / Stately docs and Visualizer
resources.why: The primary tool for modeling UI as explicit statecharts with guards, nested/parallel states, and a diagram both design and code read. The Visualizer is the shared artifact that kills design-impl drift.

resources.title: Statecharts: A Visual Formalism for Complex Systems
resources.why: The primary source for hierarchical/parallel states and the visual formalism that underpins XState and SCXML. Cite this when you want to show the idea is 35+ years load-bearing, not a JS fad.

resources.title: Thinking in Systems: A Primer
resources.why: The canonical systems-thinking text: stocks, flows, feedback loops, delays, leverage points. The 'delays relative to rate of change' idea explains double-submits and unstable UIs better than any UX book.

resources.title: Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System
resources.why: Free primary essay distilling the 12 leverage points. Use it to argue that the highest-leverage fix is often the goal/paradigm of the interface (truthful vs optimistic), not surface parameters.

resources.why: Primary reference for the correct optimistic-with-rollback mechanism and the crucial data-availability vs request-status split. Reading it teaches you exactly what to look for (or find missing) in a client codebase.

resources.title: Concurrent Optimistic Updates in React Query
resources.why: Advanced, real-world treatment of what breaks when multiple optimistic mutations race, the exact edge cases that produce 'my UI shows the wrong thing' bugs in fast SaaS apps.

resources.why: Named researcher (Microsoft Research/AutoGen) giving concrete agent-UX principles: observability/provenance, interruptibility, and streaming runtime trajectories as state. Directly maps state-machine thinking onto AI agents.

resources.title: Human-in-the-Loop Escalation Design for AI Agents
resources.why: Practitioner model for the escalation/handoff layer: risk tiers, async-first handoff, and the 'needs-approval' state gating irreversible edges. Fills the gap most agent-UX writing skips.

resources.title: Visual tests with Storybook + Chromatic
resources.why: The concrete method to turn 'every state' into a CI-enforced contract: one story per state, screenshot-diffed on every change. This is how you actually MEASURE state-render coverage.

teardownTargets.product: MetaMask / any EVM wallet transaction lifecycle
teardownTargets.why: The richest crypto state machine in the wild: submitted -> pending -> confirmed -> finalized -> failed -> dropped, plus nonce-queue blocking and the Speed Up/Cancel replacement-tx actions. Tear down whether each state has honest copy, a recovery action, and a block-explorer ground-truth link, or collapses into a dead 'pending' spinner. The nonce-queue behavior (a stuck low nonce blocks later txs) is an invisible state most UIs never surface.

teardownTargets.product: Uniswap (or any DEX) swap flow
teardownTargets.why: Multi-state approval+swap machine (quoting, needs-approval, approving, ready, submitting, pending, confirmed/failed) where slippage failures and price-impact are states, not just errors. Prime target for the optimistic-vs-truthful balance and for stale-quote-shown-as-fresh (a quote seconds old rendered as current).

teardownTargets.product: An AI agent product (Claude/ChatGPT agent mode, Cursor Composer, Devin, or Vertex/Bedrock agent UIs)
teardownTargets.why: Test observability (does it stream the plan/steps/tool calls or just spin?), interruptibility (can you pause/cancel a running trajectory?), and HITL escalation (does a risky action enter a 'needs-approval' state or auto-execute?). The 'thinking with no provenance' invisible problem lives here and is directly on Ashutosh's founder-audience beat.

teardownTargets.product: A real-time trading / prices dashboard (Coinbase, Binance, a DeFi portfolio tracker like Zapper/DeBank)
teardownTargets.why: The stale-vs-fresh and disconnect-invisibility problems concentrate here: does a dropped WebSocket surface a 'reconnecting' state or silently freeze last values? Is each number timestamped or presented as live? Perfect for demonstrating the two-axis freshness model and a truthfulness audit.

teardownTargets.product: A B2B SaaS console on a brand-new/empty account (any analytics, observability, or admin dashboard on first login)
teardownTargets.why: Best target for the UI Stack's most-skipped states: Empty (day-one onboarding) and Partial (three data points, half-configured). Shows how a powerful product reads as dead or broken before the user has generated data, the exact 'looks untrustworthy' failure founders don't see because their own account is full.

subNodes.label: The UI is a state machine whether you modeled it or not
subNodes.oneLiner: Every screen is already a finite-state machine; the only choice is whether the states are explicit and enumerated or implicit and emergent from a pile of booleans.
subNodes.body: AI/crypto products die in the states nobody named. A swap screen with isLoading, isError, isApproved, hasBalance booleans has 2^4 = 16 representable combinations but maybe 5 legal ones. The other 11 are impossible-in-reality but reachable-in-code, and that gap is exactly where 'the app looks broken / stole my money' bugs live. Modeling the machine collapses the space to only legal states.

subNodes.label: Make impossible states unrepresentable (parse, don't validate)
subNodes.oneLiner: Model state as a single discriminated union / status enum so illegal combinations cannot be constructed, instead of many independent booleans you must remember to keep consistent.
subNodes.body: David Khourshid's framing (React Rally 2017) and Kent C. Dodds' 'Stop using isLoading booleans' are the canonical statements. For a Sam-style founder, this is the difference between a demo that works and a product that survives contact with flaky RPC nodes and streaming LLM tokens: the type system, not developer discipline, guarantees you never render 'success' and 'error' at once.

subNodes.label: The UI Stack: five states per screen (Ideal, Empty, Error, Partial, Loading)
subNodes.oneLiner: Scott Hurff's rule that every screen has up to five personalities and 'Awkward UI' is what you get when you design only the Ideal one.
subNodes.body: This is the audit checklist. Founders and their engineers ship the Ideal state (the Dribbble shot) and improvise the other four under deadline. Partial state (one row of data, half-filled profile, a graph with three points) is the most-skipped and the one that makes a young AI/SaaS product feel dead on day one.

subNodes.label: Optimistic UI is a bet; truthful UI is a receipt
subNodes.oneLiner: Optimistic UI shows the intended end-state before the system confirms it, which is a loan against a promise you must be able to visibly repay (rollback) when the promise breaks.
subNodes.body: In crypto this is the single highest-stakes decision: showing a balance as updated before finality is lying if you can't unwind it. The correct model is a spectrum by irreversibility, submitted -> pending -> confirmed (N blocks) -> finalized. Optimistic is fine up to 'confirmed' for cheap/reversible actions; 'finalized' must be truthful for custody, bridging, accounting. Same logic for agents: never show 'Done' before the tool call returns.

subNodes.label: Feedback loops, stocks, and delays (Meadows systems thinking)
subNodes.oneLiner: A UI is a control system: the user acts (flow), the system accumulates state (stock), and the interface must close the loop with feedback proportional to the delay, or the user over-corrects.
subNodes.body: Donella Meadows' 'delays relative to the rate of change are a major leverage point' explains double-spends and double-submits directly: when confirmation lag (delay) exceeds the user's patience, they re-click, re-swap, re-send. The design fix is not a faster backend, it is closing the feedback loop immediately (optimistic ack + truthful pending) so the user stops driving the loop unstable.

subNodes.label: Every state transition needs an owner, a trigger, and feedback
subNodes.oneLiner: For each edge in the machine, name what event fires it, what the user sees the instant it fires, and what happens if it never fires (the timeout edge).
subNodes.body: The invisible failures are almost always missing edges: the request that never resolves, the WebSocket that silently drops, the agent step that hangs. A code-reading designer audits transitions, not screens, and the killer question is always 'what's the timeout branch, and does the UI have a state for it?'

subNodes.label: Design-state and implementation-state must be the same machine
subNodes.oneLiner: The states in the Figma file and the states in the reducer/store are two encodings of one machine; every divergence is a bug that ships.
subNodes.body: This is Ashutosh's signature edge operationalized. Designers deliver 3 states, engineers implement 6 (adding 'refetching', 'stale', 'partial-error' out of necessity), and the 3 undesigned ones get default browser styling or nothing. Reading the reducer reveals states the mockups never covered, which is the richest teardown material a designer can bring.

subNodes.label: Status enum / discriminated union over boolean soup
subNodes.oneLiner: Any async data surface. Replace {isLoading, isError, data} with status: 'idle'|'loading'|'success'|'error' plus a state-specific payload, so unreachable combos can't be typed.
subNodes.body: Example: TanStack Query already exposes this: status ('pending'|'error'|'success') plus a separate fetchStatus ('fetching'|'paused'|'idle'). The two-axis split is the pattern, one axis is 'what data do I have', the other is 'is a request in flight'. Reading a codebase for this split tells you instantly whether stale-vs-fresh was considered.

subNodes.label: Explicit statechart with XState for multi-step flows
subNodes.oneLiner: Checkout, wallet-connect, KYC, agent run loops, anything with >4 states or nested/parallel concerns. Use when transitions are conditional on current state (you can only 'confirm' from 'reviewing').
subNodes.body: Example: Model a crypto swap as states idle -> quoting -> needsApproval -> approving -> readyToSwap -> submitting -> pending -> (confirmed | failed | dropped). Guards prevent 'submit' firing from 'quoting'. The Stately visualizer renders this as a diagram you can hand to design, one artifact both disciplines read.

subNodes.label: Two-axis freshness model (data-availability x request-status)
subNodes.oneLiner: Real-time dashboards, prices, agent status, anything cached. Separate 'do I have data' from 'is it current' so you can render stale data WITH a freshness indicator instead of a blocking spinner.
subNodes.body: Example: stale-while-revalidate: show last-known price greyed with a 'as of 10s ago' timestamp and a subtle refetch shimmer, rather than either a spinner (destroys context) or silent stale data (lies). The anti-pattern it replaces is 'spinner on every refetch'.

subNodes.label: Optimistic update with visible rollback affordance
subNodes.oneLiner: Cheap, reversible, high-frequency actions (like, star, reorder, cheap on-chain actions up to 'confirmed'). Never for irreversible/custodial actions.
subNodes.body: Example: React 19 useOptimistic or TanStack onMutate->snapshot->setQueryData->onError-rollback. The load-bearing detail: the rollback must be VISIBLE and explain itself ('Couldn't save, reverted'), not a silent snap-back that makes users think they hallucinated the action.

subNodes.label: Transaction lifecycle ladder with escape hatches (crypto)
subNodes.oneLiner: Any on-chain write. Model submitted/pending/confirmed/finalized/failed/dropped as distinct states, each with its own copy and actions.
subNodes.body: Example: MetaMask's Speed Up / Cancel are same-nonce replacement transactions exposed as UI actions on the 'pending' state, plus a link to the block explorer for ground truth. The pattern: give the stuck state an action and an external source of truth, never a dead spinner.

subNodes.label: Streaming provenance for agent runs
subNodes.oneLiner: AI agents and long-running non-deterministic tasks where the trajectory is only known at runtime.
subNodes.body: Example: Victor Dibia's observability principle (BlenderLM): stream the plan, each step, tool calls, and durations as they happen. State model per step: queued -> running -> waiting-for-input -> succeeded | failed | escalated. Trust rises because reasoning becomes visible at the speed of action.

subNodes.label: Interruptibility as a first-class state (pause/resume/cancel)
subNodes.oneLiner: Expensive or risky autonomous operations. The machine must accept 'pause'/'cancel' events from most states and restore cleanly on resume.
subNodes.body: Example: Google Vertex AI ADK and BlenderLM support pausing anywhere and restoring state on resume. Design implication: every long-running state needs a reachable cancel edge, and cancel must have its own confirmed state, not just fire-and-hope.

subNodes.label: Human-in-the-loop escalation tiers
subNodes.oneLiner: Agentic products acting with real consequences (money, emails, deletes). Route by risk tier: auto-execute low-risk, confirm medium, block-and-escalate high.
subNodes.body: Example: The digitalapplied HITL model uses risk tiers with async-first handoff: the agent enters a 'needs-approval' state, surfaces context, and blocks the irreversible edge until a human fires the approve/deny event.

subNodes.label: Story-per-state (Storybook) as the state contract
subNodes.oneLiner: Any component library / design system feeding an AI/SaaS product. Write one story per legal state; the set of stories IS the enumerated machine.
subNodes.body: Example: Chromatic then screenshots every story as a visual regression baseline. A component with a loading, empty, error, partial, and ideal story has a checkable state contract; a component with only a 'default' story is an unaudited machine.

subNodes.label: Boolean soup (isLoading + isError + hasData)
subNodes.oneLiner: N booleans encode 2^N states but only a handful are legal; the rest are impossible-in-reality yet reachable-in-code. This is the root cause of 'spinner shows forever alongside data' and 'error toast over a success screen'. It also makes stale-vs-fresh inexpressible because there's no axis for it.

subNodes.label: Success-by-default / the happy-path-only mockup
subNodes.oneLiner: Designing only Hurff's Ideal state means Empty, Partial, Error, and Loading get improvised by engineers under deadline, so they inherit default browser styling or nothing. The product reads as untrustworthy precisely in the moments (first use, failure) when trust is formed.

subNodes.label: The dead spinner (loading state with no timeout branch)
subNodes.oneLiner: A spinner with no timeout edge is an impossible-to-exit state when the request hangs. There is no feedback, no retry, no escape. Hurff's own Apple TV example: a blank screen with no loading indicator makes even a frequent user fear their data is gone.

subNodes.label: Optimistic UI without rollback (or with silent rollback)
subNodes.oneLiner: Showing the end-state then failing silently, or snapping back with no explanation, teaches users the UI lies. In crypto it's catastrophic: an optimistically-updated balance that isn't truly final is indistinguishable from theft from the user's point of view.

subNodes.label: Stale-data-shown-as-fresh
subNodes.oneLiner: Cached/last-known values rendered with no freshness signal (no timestamp, no shimmer) in a real-time context. The user acts on numbers that are seconds-to-minutes old (a price, a balance, an agent status) believing they're live. This is a truthfulness bug the design never sees because in the mockup the data was always fresh.

subNodes.label: Empty state that looks identical to error or loading
subNodes.oneLiner: 'No data yet' (empty/onboarding), 'we couldn't load your data' (error), and 'still loading' are three different states with three different user actions, but collapsing them into one blank panel destroys the user's ability to know whether to wait, retry, or start creating.

subNodes.label: Toast-only error handling
subNodes.oneLiner: Errors fired as transient toasts vanish before the user reads them and leave the underlying screen in an ambiguous state. The error was an event, not a state; the screen still needs a persistent error state with a recovery action, not just a 3-second notification.

subNodes.label: One reducer, two truths (design-impl state drift)
subNodes.oneLiner: Engineers add states the design never specified (refetching, partial-error, reconnecting) and style them ad hoc. The shipped product has more states than the design system covers, so a subset always looks unfinished. Only a code-reading designer catches this by diffing the reducer against the mockups.

subNodes.label: Non-idempotent submit with no in-flight lock
subNodes.oneLiner: If the 'submitting' state doesn't disable/absorb repeat triggers, a user facing a long confirmation delay (Meadows: delay > patience) re-clicks and double-submits, double-charges, or double-sends a transaction. The missing edge is 'ignore submit while already submitting'.

subNodes.label: Missing timeout edges: the reducer handles success and error but there...
subNodes.oneLiner: Missing timeout edges: the reducer handles success and error but there is no branch for 'request never resolved', so a hung fetch leaves the UI in a permanent loading state with no recovery. Only visible by reading the async code, not the screens.

subNodes.label: Impossible states that are reachable: grep the store for independent b...
subNodes.oneLiner: Impossible states that are reachable: grep the store for independent booleans, then enumerate their 2^N combinations and mark which are legal. The illegal-but-reachable ones (loading && error, success && !data) are latent bugs the mockups can never show.

subNodes.label: Stale rendered as fresh: the component reads from cache but the design...
subNodes.oneLiner: Stale rendered as fresh: the component reads from cache but the design has no freshness indicator, so a code-reading designer must check whether fetchStatus/dataUpdatedAt is surfaced anywhere in the UI. Usually it isn't.

subNodes.label: Optimistic updates with no rollback path: onMutate writes to the cache...
subNodes.oneLiner: Optimistic updates with no rollback path: onMutate writes to the cache but onError has no rollback (or the rollback is silent). Visible only by tracing the mutation handler; the UI looks perfect until the network fails.

subNodes.label: Error events masquerading as error states: catch blocks fire a toast a...
subNodes.oneLiner: Error events masquerading as error states: catch blocks fire a toast and return, leaving the screen in its prior state. The state machine has no persistent error node, so recovery depends on a notification the user may never see.

subNodes.label: Transitions with no feedback: an event fires and state changes but not...
subNodes.oneLiner: Transitions with no feedback: an event fires and state changes but nothing renders for 100-800ms (no optimistic ack, no pending style), so the user perceives a dead click and re-fires it. The double-action bug is born in this feedback gap.

subNodes.label: State the backend has but the frontend collapses: the API returns 'par...
subNodes.oneLiner: State the backend has but the frontend collapses: the API returns 'partially_confirmed' or 'reorg_detected' or 'rate_limited' and the client maps everything non-200 to a generic 'error', discarding actionable states. Found only by reading the API contract against the client's state mapping.

subNodes.label: Reconnect/resync invisibility in real-time apps: a dropped WebSocket s...
subNodes.oneLiner: Reconnect/resync invisibility in real-time apps: a dropped WebSocket silently stops updating; the last values freeze but look live. There's no 'disconnected/reconnecting' state, so users trust a frozen screen. Detectable only by inspecting the socket lifecycle handlers.

subNodes.label: Agent 'thinking' with no provenance: the agent is in a running state b...
subNodes.oneLiner: Agent 'thinking' with no provenance: the agent is in a running state but the UI shows a generic spinner instead of the actual step/tool/plan, so users can't distinguish 'productively working' from 'stuck in a loop', which collapses trust on the first slow run.

subNodes.label: Irreversible actions gated behind reversible-action UX: a delete or an...
subNodes.oneLiner: Irreversible actions gated behind reversible-action UX: a delete or an on-chain send uses the same instant optimistic pattern as a 'like', with no confirmation state and no finality distinction, because the design treated all mutations as one class.

topics.title: Data-Heavy Screens

methods.method: First-click testing on a static screen
methods.measures: Whether users can locate the right control/metric on a dense screen on their first attempt. Optimal Workshop's analysis of millions of tree-test responses: a correct first click yields ~70% task success vs ~24% for an incorrect first click. Cheap, high-signal for scannability of a dense layout.

methods.method: Task success rate + time-on-task on realistic scenarios
methods.measures: The core outcome pair: can they complete the job (find the failing model, close the position) and how long did it take. Time-on-task is the density payoff metric; if a 'cleaner' redesign raises time-on-task for experts, you over-simplified.

methods.method: Eye-tracking / gaze plots and fixation heatmaps
methods.measures: Where attention actually lands and the scan path. NN/g's data-table gaze plots show the hierarchical zigzag (fixate col 1, jump to col 4/6, next row) that justifies frozen columns and column ordering by importance. Reveals whether your intended focal point is preattentive or lost.

methods.method: Preattentive pop-out test (250ms exposure / find-the-target)
methods.measures: Whether the one element that must be noticed is encoded in a preattentive channel. Flash the screen briefly or measure search time as distractor count grows: flat search time = preattentive (good); linear growth = serial search (your alert is buried).

methods.method: Distribution audit against the aggregate
methods.measures: Whether headline roll-ups misrepresent reality. Plot the subgroup/distribution beside every aggregate; check for Simpson reversals, bimodality, and outlier-driven means. A quantitative validation the designer can run on the actual data, not just the mock.

methods.method: State-matrix audit (design QA technique)
methods.measures: Coverage of loading/empty/zero/error/filtered-empty/partial/stale for every data region. Enumerate the states the data layer can produce (from the code) and confirm each has a designed, distinct rendering. Turns an invisible gap into a checklist.

methods.method: Live-data stress test (replay real feed at real rate)
methods.measures: Legibility and stability under production velocity: jitter, tearing, unreadable during-transition values, and whether numbers can be read while changing. Static Figma mocks never surface these; you must drive the real stream (or a replay).

methods.method: 5-second test / attention test for at-a-glance comprehension
methods.measures: What a user retains after a 5-second glance at a monitoring dashboard, matching the real 'glance' use case Few designs for. Tests whether the most important status is legible at a glance vs. requiring study.

methods.method: SUS / SEQ per task and error/misread rate
methods.measures: Post-task difficulty (Single Ease Question) and self-reported usability (SUS) for benchmarking density variants; misread rate (asking users to read specific values back) directly measures numeric legibility of formatting/alignment choices.

tactics: Lead the teardown with the invisible-failure that code-reading reveals (a silent default filter, an aggregate hiding a p99, an undesigned empty state). This is the differentiated wedge: anyone can say 'too cluttered'; only you can say 'your headline number is scoped by a hidden filter I found in the query params.'

Reframe the founder's belief from 'density = powerful' to 'attention is a fixed budget; noise is spent from the same account as signal.' Then quantify: count data-ink vs non-data-ink pixels on their current screen and show the ratio.

Ship the cheapest credibility win first: tabular-nums + right-align + consistent significant figures across every numeric column. It is a one-line CSS change, instantly visible, and signals to a fintech/AI founder that you understand numeric data at the pixel level.

Audit and design the full state matrix as a deliverable, not an afterthought. Present loading/empty/zero/error/filtered-empty side by side; most data products only have the happy path, so this alone reads as senior systems thinking.

Always pair every aggregate with its distribution in the redesign (mean + p50/p95/p99, or blended rate + per-segment). Position it as trust insurance: the number stops being a claim the user has to take on faith.

Add a freshness contract to every real-time surface: a visible 'updated Xs ago' / connection-status dot, and a defined stale threshold. Turns invisible staleness into an honest signal and directly attacks the trust leak.

Reserve color for meaning and prove it with a grayscale screenshot: if the critical status disappears in grayscale, it was color-only and will fail for colorblind users. Use the grayscale test live in the critique to make the point undeniable.

Match density to the audience explicitly (pro/terminal vs retail) and say so out loud; defend keeping density high for expert tools rather than reflexively simplifying, so you don't leak the power users chasing 'clean.'

Replace gauges/meters/traffic-lights with bullet graphs and sparklines to raise data density and free space, then reinvest the space in the distribution and state feedback the founder didn't know they were missing.
Validate the redesign with first-click + time-on-task on the real (or replayed live) data, and report the expert time-on-task delta. Numbers convince technical founders; 'feels cleaner' does not.

teardownTargets.product: Hyperliquid perpetuals trading interface
teardownTargets.why: Extreme real-time density: order book, depth chart, positions, funding, PnL, all streaming at once. Rich ground for numeric legibility (tabular figures, flicker/jitter on ticks), color-as-signal discipline, and whether the empty/stale/liquidation states are distinct. The 'powerful but does it read as trustworthy' archetype.

teardownTargets.product: dYdX v4 (perpetuals DEX)
teardownTargets.why: Same asset class, different architecture (off-chain orderbook, on-chain settlement), so a natural comparison teardown vs Hyperliquid. Good for freshness-contract analysis (is the book truly live?), aggregation of funding/PnL, and depth-chart legibility under load.

teardownTargets.product: LangSmith (LangChain) trace & eval dashboards
teardownTargets.why: AI observability with deeply nested traces, token/cost/latency tables, and eval scores: high-cardinality per-run data. Test small-multiples vs spaghetti, aggregate-vs-distribution on latency (mean hiding p99), and whether filtered/empty run lists are unambiguous. Squarely the 'Sam' AI-founder audience.

teardownTargets.product: Arize Phoenix (open-source LLM observability)
teardownTargets.why: Dense trace waterfalls, evaluation tables, and embedding/drift views; open-source means you can read the code behind the render (silent filters, client vs server sort, rounding). Ideal for the code-reading invisible-failure teardown that is Ashutosh's signature.

teardownTargets.product: PostHog (product analytics / dashboards)
teardownTargets.why: SaaS analytics with heavy aggregation (funnels, retention, trends) where SUM/AVG defaults and hidden filter scopes are everywhere. Prime target for the 'aggregation lies + silent filter + empty-vs-zero' triad, plus numeric table formatting across many tiles.

subNodes.label: Data-ink ratio (Tufte)
subNodes.oneLiner: Maximize the share of pixels that encode data; erase everything that can be removed without losing information.
subNodes.body: In AI/crypto dashboards the default is MORE chrome (gradient cards, glow borders, redundant gauges). Every non-data pixel competes with a live number a trader is scanning under time pressure. Data-ink is the objective test for 'is this element earning its place' and lets you defend deletions to a founder who thinks density = value.

subNodes.label: Signal vs. noise as a design budget (Stephen Few)
subNodes.oneLiner: A dense screen has a fixed attention budget; noise (decoration, redundant encodings, blinking) is spent from the same budget as signal.
subNodes.body: Founders equate 'powerful' with 'shows everything.' Reframing density as a zero-sum attention budget lets you argue that adding a 12th tile makes the other 11 harder to read. This is the core belief-shift for the 'looks powerful but leaks users' problem.

subNodes.label: Preattentive processing (Colin Ware)
subNodes.oneLiner: A handful of visual features (hue, position, length, orientation, motion) are perceived in <250ms before conscious attention; everything else requires serial search.
subNodes.body: It tells you WHICH channel to spend on the one thing that must pop (a liquidation warning, a failing eval) and why encoding importance in a subtle icon or a text label fails: it drops the item into slow serial search. It is the mechanism behind 'why can't users find the alert in my dense grid.'

subNodes.label: Small multiples > one busy chart
subNodes.oneLiner: Repeat the same small chart across a dimension so comparison becomes a saccade, not a memory task.
subNodes.body: AI observability (per-model, per-endpoint latency) and crypto (per-pair PnL) are inherently high-cardinality. Cramming all series into one multi-line chart creates spaghetti; small multiples keep density high while keeping each panel readable, and they scale to 20+ facets where a legend collapses.

subNodes.label: Data density is legitimate; clutter is the enemy (not density itself)
subNodes.oneLiner: High information density is a virtue when every mark is data; the failure mode is low data-density plus high decoration.
subNodes.body: Corrects the common overcorrection where designers 'simplify' a Bloomberg-style pro tool into a Robinhood toy and strip the power users' core value. Density is a target audience decision, not a universal bad. Lets you defend a dense layout to a UX-orthodox critic.

subNodes.label: Aggregation is a lossy compression (Simpson's paradox risk)
subNodes.oneLiner: Every SUM/AVG roll-up discards the distribution that could reverse the headline; the tidy number is a claim, not a fact.
subNodes.body: BI tools default to SUM()/AVG() and hide granularity. A code-reading designer can catch that a dashboard's 'avg latency 200ms' hides a bimodal p99 disaster, or that a blended conversion rate reverses per-segment. This is a trust-destroying invisible failure specific to data products.

subNodes.label: State completeness: loading ≠ empty ≠ zero ≠ error ≠ filtered-out
subNodes.oneLiner: A blank panel can mean five different things; if the UI collapses them, the user invents the scariest interpretation.
subNodes.body: In real-time data products a chart showing nothing might be: still fetching, no data exists, a true zero, a failed request, or a silent filter hiding everything. Conflating them is the #1 invisible trust leak. Only someone who reads the data-fetch code knows which states exist and must be distinguished.

subNodes.label: Tabular figures & the alignment contract
subNodes.oneLiner: Numbers compare by shape and position; proportional figures and left/center alignment break that comparison silently.
subNodes.body: This is the cheapest, highest-leverage fix in any numeric UI and an instant credibility signal to a fintech founder. Proportional digits make '1,111' narrower than '8,888', destroying scan-down comparison; tabular-nums plus right-align on the decimal restores it.

subNodes.label: Right-align numerics + tabular figures + consistent significant figures
subNodes.oneLiner: Any column of comparable numbers (price, PnL, latency, token counts, cost). Use font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums, right-align, and keep the same decimal precision down a column so magnitudes line up.
subNodes.body: Example: A crypto positions table where $1,234.50 and $88.00 right-align on the decimal, both showing 2 dp, so a trader scans the ones/tens/hundreds columns as vertical stripes.

subNodes.label: Sparklines and in-row micro-charts (data-words)
subNodes.oneLiner: When each row needs trend context but a full chart per row would blow the density budget. Embed a word-sized line/bar showing the last N points inline.
subNodes.body: Example: An order-row sparkline of recent price, or a per-model latency sparkline in an AI observability table, giving trend without a drill-down click.

subNodes.label: Small multiples grid
subNodes.oneLiner: Comparing the same metric across many entities (models, endpoints, trading pairs, cohorts) where a single overlaid chart becomes spaghetti.
subNodes.body: Example: A 4x5 grid of identical mini line charts, one per model, shared y-axis, so an outlier model's latency spike pops via position/shape.

subNodes.label: Bullet graph instead of gauge/meter (Few)
subNodes.oneLiner: Showing a measure against a target/threshold band in minimal space. Replaces circular gauges that waste space and show one number.
subNodes.body: Example: A KPI strip where each metric is a horizontal bullet: actual bar, target tick, and qualitative bands, packing 6 KPIs into the space one gauge would take.

subNodes.label: Frozen header + frozen first column + zebra/hover row highlight
subNodes.oneLiner: Tables taller/wider than the viewport where users lose their row while scanning across many columns (the eye-tracking 'hierarchical zigzag' pattern).
subNodes.body: Example: Freeze the human-readable identifier column and header; add subtle drop shadow so they read as floating above the scroll body, plus hover-row highlight to keep place.

subNodes.label: Explicit active-filter chips + result-count with reset
subNodes.oneLiner: Any filtered/queried view, especially when a filter can reduce results to zero. Always surface which filters are active and why the view is empty.
subNodes.body: Example: A row of removable filter chips above the table plus 'Showing 0 of 4,812  -  3 filters active [clear]' so an empty grid never reads as broken.

subNodes.label: Distinct five-state rendering for every data region
subNodes.oneLiner: Every async, real-time, or filterable panel. Design skeleton (loading), empty-no-data, true-zero, error-with-retry, and filtered-empty as separate visuals.
subNodes.body: Example: Skeleton shimmer while streaming; 'No trades yet' with CTA for genuine empty; '0.00' rendered as a real value; red retry card on fetch fail; 'No matches for current filters' when filtered.

subNodes.label: Direct labeling over legends in dense charts
subNodes.oneLiner: Multi-series charts where a legend forces a color-matching round-trip that spends serial attention. Label lines at their endpoints.
subNodes.body: Example: Endpoint labels on a multi-line cost-over-time chart so the eye never leaves the data to decode a color key.

subNodes.label: Semantic color reserved for meaning, neutral for the rest
subNodes.oneLiner: When up/down, profit/loss, healthy/degraded must pop. Keep the field grayscale so the few colored marks are preattentive; never color everything.
subNodes.body: Example: Green/red only on PnL deltas and only on the sign, with a non-color redundant cue (arrow/sign) for colorblind users; the rest of the table stays neutral.

subNodes.label: Gauge/meter/traffic-light dashboards
subNodes.oneLiner: One number per large widget (terrible data density), red/green fails for ~8% of men who are colorblind, and decorative bezels/needles are pure non-data-ink. Few's whole critique. Common in crypto 'analytics' skins that look impressive and inform poorly.

subNodes.label: Rainbow-everything / semantic color inflation
subNodes.oneLiner: When every column is colored, nothing is preattentive; the one cell that should scream (a liquidation, a failing guardrail) is camouflaged. Color stops being signal and becomes texture.

subNodes.label: Proportional figures + center/left-aligned numbers
subNodes.oneLiner: Digit widths differ so columns don't line up; the eye can't compare magnitudes by position, forcing slow digit-by-digit reading. Silent because it 'looks fine' in a mock with tidy sample data.

subNodes.label: Flicker/jitter on real-time updates
subNodes.oneLiner: Animating the text node width (non-tabular digits) shifts neighboring cells on every tick; rapid full-value repaints cause visual tearing and make numbers physically hard to read while they change. Erodes trust in a live feed.

subNodes.label: Silent filters and hidden default scopes
subNodes.oneLiner: A default date range, a hidden 'exclude test traffic' toggle, or a persisted filter makes the whole screen lie without any on-screen cue. The user sees a confident number that is quietly scoped. Classic invisible trust leak.

subNodes.label: Aggregation without distribution (mean-only)
subNodes.oneLiner: A single average hides bimodality, outliers, and Simpson's-paradox reversals. 'Avg response 200ms' next to a p99 of 9s is technically true and operationally catastrophic. BI defaults encourage it.

subNodes.label: The undifferentiated blank panel
subNodes.oneLiner: Loading, empty, zero, filtered-out, and error all render as the same nothing. Users default to the worst reading ('it's broken') and churn. The states exist in the data layer but not in the UI.

subNodes.label: Spaghetti multi-line charts / legend overload
subNodes.oneLiner: Beyond ~4-5 series, overlaid lines cross and colors become indistinguishable; the legend forces constant color-matching. High cardinality (per-model, per-pair) makes this the default failure in observability tools.

subNodes.label: Over-simplification of a pro tool
subNodes.oneLiner: Stripping density to chase 'clean' removes the exact multi-panel, at-a-glance power a trader/SRE needs, pushing them back to Bloomberg/terminal. Density is an audience decision; sanitizing it leaks the power users.

subNodes.label: Precision theater (too many significant figures)
subNodes.oneLiner: Showing $1,234.56789 or 99.99997% implies false precision, widens columns, and slows scanning. Noise dressed as rigor; also breaks alignment when precision varies row to row.

subNodes.label: Silent filter/default-scope: a persisted or default filter (date range...
subNodes.oneLiner: Silent filter/default-scope: a persisted or default filter (date range, 'exclude internal', a saved segment) quietly scopes every number on the screen with no visible chip. Only reading the query/state code reveals the headline is conditional.

subNodes.label: Aggregation hides a reversing subgroup: the roll-up uses SUM/AVG and t...
subNodes.oneLiner: Aggregation hides a reversing subgroup: the roll-up uses SUM/AVG and the per-segment trend reverses (Simpson's paradox), or a bimodal distribution is flattened to a meaningless mean. Invisible unless you inspect the GROUP BY and the raw distribution.

subNodes.label: Empty state ambiguity in the data layer: the fetch can resolve to null...
subNodes.oneLiner: Empty state ambiguity in the data layer: the fetch can resolve to null, [], 200-with-empty-body, a timeout, or a true zero, but the component maps all of them to one blank view. A code-reader sees the branch that was never designed.

subNodes.label: Stale-while-revalidate lies: cached data renders as live with no 'last...
subNodes.oneLiner: Stale-while-revalidate lies: cached data renders as live with no 'last updated' timestamp or freshness indicator; the WebSocket dropped and the number froze, but the UI still looks real-time. Requires knowing the data-fetching/caching strategy to catch.

subNodes.label: Client-side rounding/formatting drift: the API returns full precision,...
subNodes.oneLiner: Client-side rounding/formatting drift: the API returns full precision, the UI rounds for display, and a sum of displayed values no longer equals the displayed total (1+1=3 rounding). Visible only if you compare raw payload to rendered cells.

subNodes.label: Number jitter from proportional fonts: layout shifts on every tick bec...
subNodes.oneLiner: Number jitter from proportional fonts: layout shifts on every tick because digits aren't tabular; imperceptible in a static mock, obvious only under a live stream, so it survives design review and ships.

subNodes.label: Sorting/pagination that sorts only the current page: the table sorts t...
subNodes.oneLiner: Sorting/pagination that sorts only the current page: the table sorts the loaded 50 rows, not the full dataset, so 'top by volume' is wrong. You catch it by reading whether sort is a server param or a client array method.

subNodes.label: Color-only encoding of critical state: profit/loss or pass/fail carrie...
subNodes.oneLiner: Color-only encoding of critical state: profit/loss or pass/fail carried purely by red/green with no sign/icon/shape redundancy; fails silently for colorblind users and in grayscale exports. A systems view checks for a redundant channel.

subNodes.label: Throttled/debounced real-time updates masquerading as tick-by-tick: th...
subNodes.oneLiner: Throttled/debounced real-time updates masquerading as tick-by-tick: the feed is sampled every 2s but presented as continuous, hiding intra-window volatility that a trader is actually being paid to see.

subNodes.label: Timezone and unit ambiguity: timestamps rendered in server UTC vs. vie...
subNodes.oneLiner: Timezone and unit ambiguity: timestamps rendered in server UTC vs. viewer local, or values in wei/gwei/ETH or ms/s without a unit label; the number is 'right' and the interpretation is wrong. Caught by reading the formatter, not the mock.

topics.title: Dashboards & Entry Points
topics.fullTitle: Dashboards & multiple entry points / multi-intent IA

methods.method: Tree testing (Treejack / UserZoom)
methods.measures: Findability of the IA independent of visual design: direct success rate (found without backtracking), indirect success rate (found after up/down navigation), time-on-task, and tier-1 first-click distribution. Isolates whether the taxonomy/labels are the problem vs. the layout.

methods.method: First-click / click testing
methods.measures: Whether the first interaction lands in the right region. Diagnostic rule of thumb: if ~60%+ of participants first-click the same wrong node, the failure is a structural or labeling error at that branch, and first click strongly predicts eventual task success.

methods.method: Closed card sorting
methods.measures: Whether users can place content into YOUR proposed categories (validates category names/fit). Run alongside a click test: good card-sort + bad click-test means the labels are fine but the layout is broken (NN/G's multi-method triangulation).

methods.method: Moderated task-based usability testing
methods.measures: The combined IA + UI + copy + interaction failure on the real interface, including where the primary action is missed and where the evaluation gulf opens (users say 'wait, did that work?'). Explains the WHY behind quantitative failures.

methods.method: Feature-adoption funnel: Exposed → Activated → Used → Used again
