methods.measures: Where users fall out per feature/entry point (Amplitude/Mixpanel/Pendo). Reveals whether a multi-intent dashboard is exposing a feature but failing to activate it, i.e., the entry point is present but not persuasive.

methods.method: Time-to-value / time-to-first-key-action
methods.measures: Elapsed time from first login to the 'aha' action the dashboard exists to enable. A rising TTV or high single-session-then-churn (the ~40-60% open-once cohort) flags a broken first-run/empty state or a buried primary action.

methods.method: Path / flow analysis + rage-click and back-button telemetry
methods.measures: Actual navigation paths versus the intended one: loops, competing entry points converging on one route, and rage-clicks on non-interactive elements. Surfaces the invisible 'multiple doors to one job' and 'state resets on back' problems in production.

tactics: Write the one-sentence 'question this screen answers' for every dashboard and region before designing; delete or demote any widget that doesn't serve it. Use it as the acceptance test in design review.

Map 2-4 context scenarios (Goodwin) to a single shared shell: one overview, role-conditioned top module and one role-specific primary action. Resist shipping N separate home screens; consistency of the spine is what teammates and support rely on.

Give every entry point a gradient: exactly one primary action, everything else visually secondary. If two actions must coexist, make the design system enforce a single 'primary' variant per view so primacy can't drift by accident.

Treat the URL as the source of truth for view state: encode filter/time/selection/tab, offer named saved views with clean permalinks. This turns 'share my view' from a support ticket into a paste, and is a concrete trust signal for collaborative teams.

Kill the blank first-run: seed labeled sample data or an interactive build-your-dashboard step, and strip the empty state to one obvious action visible from the first pixel. Measure the change with time-to-first-key-action.

For AI/agent and crypto surfaces, close the evaluation gulf explicitly: stream state (plan, current step, cost), classify actions by risk, gate medium/high-risk ones behind explicit approval, and never let optimistic UI mask a failed/irreversible write. This is the direct fix for 'powerful but untrustworthy.'

Push decisions, don't just display them: pair the dashboard with alerts that carry context (why it moved, who's impacted, suggested next step) routed to where the user already works, so the product earns trust by triaging for them.
Add a Cmd+K command palette as a findability safety net so you can keep the visible surface sparse; it lets deep IA stay reachable without cramming nav, and signals product maturity to power users.

Run tree test + first-click + closed card sort simultaneously and remotely before a redesign; the cheap triangulation tells you whether to fix labels, structure, or layout, and stops panic-driven knee-jerk rebuilds.

Audit the code, not just the comps: grep the route table for duplicate destinations (competing entry points), check whether view state is in the router or trapped in useState, and confirm role gating is enforced server-side. These are the teardown findings only a code-reading designer produces.

resources.title: Information Dashboard Design: Displaying Data for At-a-Glance Monitoring (2nd ed.)
resources.why: The canonical definition of a dashboard and the 13 named design mistakes; still the sharpest weapon against the dumping-ground anti-pattern and the 'is this actually a dashboard' question.

resources.title: Designing for the Digital Age: How to Create Human-Centered Products and Services
resources.why: The definitive text on persona + context-scenario-driven design for complex enterprise/analytical apps; the antidote to org-chart/schema-mirrored IA in multi-intent dashboards.

resources.title: Low Findability and Discoverability: Four Testing Methods to Identify the Causes
resources.why: Primary-source method guide distinguishing findability vs discoverability and showing how to triangulate tree test + card sort + click test + usability test to locate the real cause. Directly operationalizes measurement for this cluster.

resources.title: 4 UX Design Principles for Autonomous Multi-Agent AI Systems
resources.why: Named researcher, primary source. Capability discovery, observability/provenance, interruptibility, and cost-aware delegation are the exact vocabulary for designing trustworthy AI agent consoles. Includes a built reference implementation (BlenderLM).

resources.title: Badass: Making Users Awesome
resources.why: Reframes multi-intent design from feature-count to user-outcome and names 'cognitive leaks' - the mechanism behind decision fatigue on overloaded dashboards. High belief-shift content for posts.

resources.title: Dashboard Design UX Patterns (Best Practices)
resources.why: The most systems-literate free pattern catalog: names the drill-in patterns (details page, master-detail), the 'data seems random and unfocused' anti-pattern, and Jira-style custom-dashboard flows. Directly reusable teardown vocabulary.

resources.title: Progressive Disclosure
resources.why: The original formal treatment of progressive disclosure and its cost/benefit tradeoff; the theoretical backing for Summary→Context→Details tiering at scale.

resources.title: The Eyes Have It: A Task by Data Type Taxonomy for Information Visualizations
resources.why: Primary source for 'Overview first, zoom and filter, details-on-demand' - the load-bearing mantra for drill-down architecture. Citing the original paper (not a blog restatement) is on-brand for a code-reading designer.

resources.title: The Design of Everyday Things (Gulfs of Execution & Evaluation)
resources.why: The gulf-of-evaluation framing is the most precise way to explain WHY async/crypto/agent dashboards 'feel untrustworthy' - the system changes state without telling the user in actionable terms.

resources.title: Personas vs. Jobs-to-Be-Done
resources.why: Clarifies when to structure a multi-intent dashboard around personas vs. JTBD - the core decision behind role-based views vs. task-based entry points.

resources.title: Why Employees Ignore Dashboards - and What Replaces Them
resources.why: Sharp belief-shift argument that passive pull-dashboards lose to pushed decision-workflows (alert + context + next step); good provocation source for an opinion post, even if vendor-flavored.

resources.title: cmdk (command palette) + Linear/Vercel/Stripe premium-UI teardowns
resources.why: Reference implementation and analysis of Cmd+K as a secondary entry point and of interaction-dense-but-sparse dashboards. Concrete study material for the 'multiple entry points done well' pattern.

teardownTargets.product: MetaMask browser-extension home + transaction confirmation flow
teardownTargets.why: Powerful but classic 'reads as untrustworthy': the home screen and confirm modal have a large evaluation gulf (network state, permissions, gas, irreversibility) and treat the sign action like an ordinary CTA. Rich territory for a consequence-disclosure and trust-boundary teardown.

teardownTargets.product: An AI agent console (e.g., AutoGen Studio, or an OpenAI/Anthropic-style agent run view)
teardownTargets.why: Test Dibia's four principles directly: can the user observe the run trajectory, interrupt it, see cost, and know which actions are risky? Most consoles show a chat log but fail observability/interruptibility - a strong 'invisible problem' post about non-deterministic long-running state.

teardownTargets.product: Datadog or Grafana default dashboard landing
teardownTargets.why: Textbook dumping-ground vs. progressive-disclosure tension: dozens of tiles, competing entry points, uniform-urgency alerts. Great for demonstrating 'one screen, one question' and URL/deep-link state findings a code-reader would catch.

teardownTargets.product: Jira / Linear project home (multi-role B2B admin)
teardownTargets.why: Direct multi-intent IA study: Jira leans on heavy user-customizable gadget dashboards (personalization-vs-consistency failure mode), Linear leans on a sparse shared shell + Cmd+K. Tearing down both side by side is a ready-made belief-shift post.

teardownTargets.product: A crypto exchange or DeFi dashboard first-run (e.g., Coinbase or Uniswap home for a brand-new/empty account)
teardownTargets.why: Combines the highest-stakes empty state (zero balance, zero history) with a trust boundary and multiple competing entry points (buy, swap, connect, earn). Ideal for a first-run + primary-action + trust teardown skewed to crypto.

subNodes.label: Few's 'at-a-glance monitoring' test
subNodes.oneLiner: A true dashboard displays the most important info for an objective on a single screen, monitored at a glance; if it needs study, it is a report wearing a dashboard's clothes.
subNodes.body: AI/crypto consoles routinely fail this: they dump every metric a backend can emit. Applying Few's definition lets you argue for cutting, not adding, and forces the question 'monitored toward WHAT objective' before any widget survives.

subNodes.label: Overview-first, then zoom-and-filter, then details-on-demand (Shneiderman's mantra)
subNodes.oneLiner: Overview first, zoom and filter, then details-on-demand; each layer answers a bigger question with fewer pixels than the layer below.
subNodes.body: It is the load-bearing skeleton for progressive disclosure at scale. For a multi-intent dashboard it means the landing view is a shared overview and each role's task lives one deliberate drill-down away, so you serve many intents without N separate home screens.

subNodes.label: One screen answers one question
subNodes.oneLiner: Each dashboard (or dashboard region) should answer exactly one core question; if it answers three, users answer none.
subNodes.body: This is the antidote to 'we have the data so show it.' In B2B admin panels and agent consoles, naming the single question per region is what separates a decision surface from a data-dump, and it gives you a falsifiable spec to test against.

subNodes.label: Gulfs of Execution and Evaluation (Norman) applied to state
subNodes.oneLiner: Execution gulf = 'what do I do next'; evaluation gulf = 'what just happened / what is true now'; both widen on live, async, or agentic dashboards.
subNodes.body: Crypto (pending tx, mempool) and AI agents (non-deterministic long-running runs) have huge evaluation gulfs. Untrustworthy feel is usually an unbridged evaluation gulf: the system changed state and never told the user in terms they can act on.

subNodes.label: Build badass users, not badass products (Kathy Sierra)
subNodes.oneLiner: Design for the user's post-tool competence and outcome, not for feature completeness; minimize cognitive leaks between them and the win.
subNodes.body: Reframes 'multi-intent' from 'more features per screen' to 'each entry point advances a real outcome.' A crypto founder's users don't want a wallet home screen, they want to feel safely in control of funds; that reframing changes what the entry point must do.

subNodes.label: Personas + context scenarios drive IA, not org chart (Kim Goodwin / Cooper)
subNodes.oneLiner: Derive the dashboard's structure from context scenarios of 2-4 real personas' goals, not from the backend's data model or the company's team structure.
subNodes.body: Most enterprise dashboards mirror the database schema or the internal team layout (Conway's law leaking into UI). Scenario-driven IA is why a multi-intent dashboard can feel coherent instead of like several teams' tabs stapled together.

subNodes.label: Dashboard as pull vs. decision-workflow as push
subNodes.oneLiner: A passive dashboard makes users remember to look and translate numbers into action; the trust-winning move is pushing the decision (alert + context + suggested next step) to where they already work.
subNodes.body: 40-60% of B2B trial users open once and never return; a dashboard that requires a return visit and mental translation loses them. For AI/crypto, tying state changes to actionable notifications (not just a badge) is the difference between 'looks powerful' and 'I trust it to tell me when it matters.'

subNodes.label: The connect/first-action moment is a trust boundary, not a CTA
subNodes.oneLiner: The first high-stakes action (connect wallet, grant agent permissions, first drill-down) is where the user decides whether to expose risk; treat it as a consequence-disclosure moment.
subNodes.body: In crypto and agent products the primary entry point asks the user to accept irreversible or costly consequences. Designing it like an ordinary marketing CTA (big button, no consequence framing) is a primary source of the 'reads as untrustworthy' complaint.

subNodes.label: Three-tier disclosure: Summary → Context → Details
subNodes.oneLiner: Any dense multi-intent dashboard. Top: 3-5 KPIs answering the one question. Middle: trend/context charts. Bottom or drill-in: granular tables. Use when you must serve at-a-glance monitoring AND investigation from one surface.
subNodes.body: Example: Stripe's payments home (balance + key trend up top, transactions table on drill-in). Datadog dashboards with summary tiles linking to context links / detail views.

subNodes.label: Shared overview + role-conditioned modules
subNodes.oneLiner: When multiple roles share one product but have different primary tasks. Keep one consistent overview; conditionally reorder/surface modules and the primary action by role, rather than shipping N disjoint home screens.
subNodes.body: Example: Role-relevant content makes users ~3x more likely to activate (SaaS onboarding data). A CS manager and an admin see the same shell, different default 'top' module and primary CTA.

subNodes.label: Command palette (Cmd+K) as a universal secondary entry point
subNodes.oneLiner: When IA is necessarily deep (many objects/actions) and you cannot surface everything in nav. The palette is a findability safety net and a power-user express lane, not a replacement for good IA.
subNodes.body: Example: Linear, Vercel, Notion, Raycast: create/assign/navigate from one fuzzy-search surface. Lets you keep the visual dashboard sparse while keeping every action reachable in two keystrokes.

subNodes.label: Peek → detail progression (drawer/side-panel before full page)
subNodes.oneLiner: When users triage a list and need detail on some items without losing list context. Use a side panel/drawer for reversible inspection; reserve full detail pages for deep work or shareable/deep-linkable views.
subNodes.body: Example: Incident/alert queues, agent run lists: click a row, a drawer shows the run trace; 'open full view' for the deep-linkable page.

subNodes.label: Seeded / demo state instead of a blank first-run
subNodes.oneLiner: First login before the user has data. Replace the empty canvas with sample data (clearly labeled, removable), a single obvious action, or a build-your-own-dashboard onboarding step.
subNodes.body: Example: The zero-data dashboard is the highest-stakes empty state in the product; strip it to one action ('Connect your first integration') visible from the first pixel.

subNodes.label: URL-encoded, shareable view state
subNodes.oneLiner: Whenever a user builds a filtered/time-scoped view others will need. Encode filters, time range, and selection in the URL and offer named saved views with clean permalinks.
subNodes.body: Example: Datadog context links, Metabase/Superset saved views. A team lead pastes a link instead of describing a filter recipe; this is invisible IA that a code-reading designer specs deliberately.

subNodes.label: Cost/risk-classified confirmation (agent & crypto)
subNodes.oneLiner: When an entry point triggers actions with side effects. Classify actions low/medium/high risk; auto-run low, require explicit approval for medium/high; always show reversibility and cost before commit.
subNodes.body: Example: Victor Dibia's 'cost-aware delegation'; wallet transaction confirmations that state the consequence, fee, and irreversibility rather than a bare 'Confirm'.

subNodes.label: Dashboard as dumping ground ('we have it, so show it')
subNodes.oneLiner: Every added chart signals importance, so N charts destabilize the user into assuming all N matter; diminishing returns turn into negative returns. The user cannot infer the one question, so they answer none and leave. Pencil & Paper call this 'data seems random and unfocused.'

subNodes.label: No clear primary action / competing CTAs
subNodes.oneLiner: When several buttons look equally weighted, the entry point has no gradient; users hit decision fatigue choosing dropdowns/tabs/toggles and never reach the actual decision ('salad bar effect'). Trust erodes because the product does not seem to know what the user is there to do.

subNodes.label: Multiple competing entry points to the same job
subNodes.oneLiner: Three doors to the same task (nav item + dashboard card + modal) fragment analytics, split muscle memory, and create 'which one is canonical?' doubt. A code-reading designer spots this as duplicated routes/handlers pointing at one destination.

subNodes.label: Org-chart / schema-mirrored IA
subNodes.oneLiner: Structuring nav around internal teams or DB tables (Conway's law in the UI) forces users to learn your org to find their task. Fails tree tests because category names are producer-language, not user-goal language.

subNodes.label: Alerts without context / uniform-urgency badges
subNodes.oneLiner: When every alert looks equally urgent, none is urgent. Isolated data points with no 'why it moved / who's impacted / what to do' push the diagnosis offline, so the dashboard becomes a static report nobody trusts to prioritize for them.

subNodes.label: Blank empty state as default first-run
subNodes.oneLiner: A zero-data canvas is where 40-60% of trial users decide the product isn't worth it. It shows the skeleton before any value, maximizing the evaluation gulf at the exact moment trust is most fragile.

subNodes.label: Personalization that erodes a shared mental model
subNodes.oneLiner: Full drag-and-drop customization sounds empowering but destroys cross-user consistency (support, docs, and teammates can no longer say 'click the top-right card'), and most users never configure it, so defaults still carry the load. Customize the last mile, standardize the spine.

subNodes.label: Ephemeral state that can't be linked or restored
subNodes.oneLiner: If filters/time-range/selection live only in component state and never in the URL, users can't share, bookmark, or return to a view; a code-reading designer catches this as state trapped in useState instead of the router. Reads as fragile and untrustworthy for collaborative work.

subNodes.label: State lives in component memory, not the URL: filters, tab, time-range...
subNodes.oneLiner: State lives in component memory, not the URL: filters, tab, time-range, and row selection are trapped in local state, so refresh, back-button, and share all silently reset the view. Only visible if you read the router/state code or hammer the back button.

subNodes.label: Loading and empty states are the same component with no distinction: a...
subNodes.oneLiner: Loading and empty states are the same component with no distinction: a slow query renders as 'no data,' so users conclude a feature is broken or empty when it is merely pending. Requires reading the fetch/skeleton logic to catch.

subNodes.label: The 'primary' action is a styling accident, not an information-archite...
subNodes.oneLiner: The 'primary' action is a styling accident, not an information-architecture decision: two buttons share the same variant class, so visual primacy drifts per screen. A code reader sees identical component props where intent should differ.

subNodes.label: Multiple routes resolve to the same destination: nav link, dashboard c...
subNodes.oneLiner: Multiple routes resolve to the same destination: nav link, dashboard card, and a modal all navigate to /settings/integrations, fragmenting analytics and muscle memory. Only visible by grepping the route table against the UI.

subNodes.label: Optimistic UI hides failed writes: the dashboard shows the new state i...
subNodes.oneLiner: Optimistic UI hides failed writes: the dashboard shows the new state instantly, but the mutation failed and the rollback is silent or a toast that already dismissed, so the user trusts a value that isn't real (acute in crypto tx and agent actions).

subNodes.label: Role gating is done in the frontend only: modules are hidden with CSS/...
subNodes.oneLiner: Role gating is done in the frontend only: modules are hidden with CSS/conditional render while the API still returns the data, which is both a trust and a security leak a systems designer flags immediately.

subNodes.label: Real-time widgets poll on independent intervals: KPIs on one screen re...
subNodes.oneLiner: Real-time widgets poll on independent intervals: KPIs on one screen refresh at different cadences, so two tiles disagree for a few seconds and users can't tell if it's lag or a real discrepancy. Invisible unless you inspect network timing.

subNodes.label: Deep-link and default landing disagree: a shared URL restores a filter...
subNodes.oneLiner: Deep-link and default landing disagree: a shared URL restores a filtered view, but the app's default route redirects authenticated users elsewhere, so shared links intermittently dead-end. Caught only by tracing redirect guards.

topics.title: Task-Based SaaS
topics.fullTitle: Task-based design for SaaS (the loop, not the screen)

methods.method: JTBD switch interviews (Moesta timeline)
methods.measures: Reconstructs the demand-side timeline of the last ~10 recent adopters (first thought, passive/active looking, deciding, first use) to surface the push/pull/anxiety/habit forces and the specific struggling moment the product was hired for. Reveals the real job the task flow must serve.

methods.method: Activation event discovery via correlation analysis
methods.measures: Regress early behaviors against week-N retention across cohorts to find the action(s) whose completers retain sharply better (the Facebook '7 friends/10 days' method). Output is a candidate activation metric, validated by lift in retention, not intuition.

methods.method: Retention-curve-flattening / cohort analysis
methods.measures: Whether cohorts settle to a non-zero floor (durable value) or decay to zero (no real value). The floor level matters less than the fact of flattening. This is the trailing truth that any activation metric must predict.

methods.method: Sean Ellis 40% must-have survey
methods.measures: Leading indicator of product-market fit: % of active users who would be 'very disappointed' to lose the product. Segment the 'very disappointed' cohort to find who the strongest job fit is and what activation path they took.

methods.method: Funnel + drop-off instrumentation per loop step
methods.measures: Step-by-step conversion between signup and each activation milestone (setup, aha, habit), exposing exactly which loop step is the gutter. Distinct from a single activation rate because it localizes the leak (e.g., 70% of web3 drop happens at seed-phrase backup).

methods.method: First-click / task-success usability testing on the real first-run
methods.measures: Whether a genuinely new user (empty account, no priming) can start and close the core loop unaided. Josh Elman's 'try your own onboarding' + tracing the last 20 converters. Surfaces dead ends and gulf-of-execution failures that heatmaps hide.

methods.method: Session replay filtered to rage/dead-click and abandonment
methods.measures: Where users hesitate, repeat actions, or abandon after a 'successful' action, exposing loops that closed on the backend but not in the user's perception (evaluation-gulf failures).

methods.method: Agent trust telemetry: intervention, override, and correction rate
methods.measures: For AI agents, how often humans pause/override/redo the agent and whether corrections reduce future interventions. Rising re-brief rate signals the loop isn't carrying state; falling override rate over time signals calibrated trust forming.

methods.method: Instrumentation audit against domain events (code-reading method)
methods.measures: Verifies analytics events are bound to real domain state changes (order created, funds moved) rather than UI mounts or route changes, so the measured funnel reflects actual task completion. This is the systems-designer's differentiator.

tactics: Define one North Star loop per product and one activation event that provably predicts retention; ruthlessly delete anything between signup and that event. If a step doesn't reduce anxiety or produce value, it's latency, cut it.
Redesign every success state as a loop-closer: state read-back (show the thing that changed) + the single most likely next action. Ban terminal 'Done' screens that return to an empty dashboard.

Audit the evaluation half of the loop in code: for each core action, confirm the UI re-renders the new domain state and surfaces the failure path, not just the happy path. This is the concrete form of 'I read the code before I judge the design' for trust.

Convert onboarding from a feature tour into anxiety retirement: name the top 2-3 fears for the category (AI: 'it will hallucinate and I'll be blamed'; crypto: 'I'll lose funds irreversibly') and put a specific loop step that retires each fear before asking for commitment.

Defer or fake setup: sample data, templates, and email/social login instead of blocking config; land first value inside the 5-minute budget, then invite the deeper setup as an upsell to a second loop.

For agents, ship an editable plan + a persistent, visible action log, and make interrupting cost ~zero (pause/undo always available). Scale confirmation friction to blast radius. Present calibrated uncertainty, not false confidence.

Model the object graph (OOUX ORCA) before drawing flows so navigation is stable and matches the codebase, then choreograph task loops over it. Use object-oriented IA for the map, task-based loops for the journey.

Instrument setup/aha/habit as three separate funnel milestones and review them against the cohort retention curve weekly; treat a rising activation rate with a still-decaying curve as a red flag, not a win.

Run the teardown as a leak audit: walk the real first-run of a target product with an empty account, mark every open gulf (action with no legible result), every dead end, and every feature-named nav item that hides a job. That artifact is both the post and the sales pitch to a 'Sam'.

resources.title: The Design of Everyday Things (esp. the Seven Stages of Action, Gulf of Execution & Evaluation)
resources.why: The primary source for 'the loop.' The two gulfs are the exact vocabulary for why a task feels broken when feedback/confirmation is missing. Load-bearing for the whole cluster.

resources.title: Badass: Making Users Awesome
resources.why: The canonical 'compelling context' argument: users want to be badass at their job, not at your tool. Reframes task design around felt user competence, which is the trust lever.

resources.title: Demand-Side Sales 101 / Jobs-to-be-Done switch interviews & Forces of Progress
resources.source: Bob Moesta (with Chris Spiek, The Re-Wired Group)
resources.why: Primary source for applying JTBD to real adoption: the switch timeline and push/pull/anxiety/habit forces that decide whether a task loop ever starts. jobstobedone.org has the raw interviews.

resources.title: The Elements of User Onboarding + UserOnboard teardowns
resources.why: The definitive practitioner source on first-run design and empty states as onboarding. The annotated teardowns are a direct template for Ashutosh's teardown pillar.

resources.title: Object-Oriented UX (OOUX) and the ORCA process
resources.why: The 'nouns before verbs' method that reconciles task-based flows with a stable object model, and the reason it maps cleanly onto how engineers structure code, exactly Ashutosh's edge.

resources.title: The Bowling Alley Framework (straight-line onboarding)
resources.why: The most concrete named pattern for onboarding-as-task-completion: line to value, product + human bumpers over the gutters. Directly actionable for activation redesigns.

resources.title: Every Product Needs a North Star Metric + the 4 Stages of Activation (setup/aha/habit)
resources.why: Operationalizes activation measurement into ordered milestones and ties them to a North Star. The measurement backbone for this cluster.

resources.title: The Sean Ellis 40% test + retention-curve-flattening as PMF signal
resources.why: The must-have survey as a leading indicator plus the cohort-curve-flattening truth test; how to validate that your activation event actually predicts durable value.

resources.title: Josh Elman on onboarding: 'trace the last 20 converters' and don't treat onboarding as one flow
resources.why: Sharp, primary-source tactics for discovering the activation path empirically and designing onboarding as multiple loops across sessions.

resources.title: How to design agentic products
resources.why: Advanced, specific principles for agent task loops: transparency of intent/state, cheap human control, feedback that carries state, and the 'don't re-brief every time' anti-pattern. Directly on the AI-agent brief.

resources.title: Frictionless Web3 UX / DeFi first-activation patterns (embedded wallets, 70% drop at seed phrase)
resources.why: Hard, measurable crypto onboarding data: where the loop breaks (seed-phrase backup, post-wallet-connect) and the embedded-wallet fix. Ammunition for a crypto teardown.

resources.title: Intercom on Onboarding + Bob Moesta on JTBD (Intercom podcast/book)
resources.source: Intercom (Des Traynor et al.) with Bob Moesta
resources.why: A field-tested synthesis of JTBD + onboarding from a company that shipped it, with the Moesta interview as primary source. Good bridge from theory to SaaS practice.

teardownTargets.product: A crypto DeFi dApp first transaction flow (e.g. Uniswap or a Solana DEX) from wallet-connect through swap confirmation
teardownTargets.why: Textbook loop-that-never-closes and confirmation-friction failures: wallet-connect works but 60-90% churn before a first transaction; the post-connect moment is a dead end, signing dialogs give opaque previews, and success/confirmation state is often illegible. Perfect 'powerful but untrustworthy' case, with public drop-off benchmarks to cite.

teardownTargets.product: An AI agent product's task flow (e.g. an autonomous coding or ops agent, or an AI research/agent mode)
teardownTargets.why: Shows the evaluation-gulf and re-brief anti-patterns: agent acts but the plan isn't editable, the action log isn't surfaced, uncertainty is hidden behind confident copy, and undo/interrupt is expensive. Ideal to demonstrate calibrated-trust mechanisms (editable plan, validation feed, friction-to-stakes).

teardownTargets.product: A feature-rich B2B SaaS onboarding (e.g. Jira, HubSpot, or a data/observability tool's first-run)
teardownTargets.why: Classic feature-based-IA-hides-the-job plus onboarding-as-tour: heavy setup latency, tour that inflates completion while activation stays flat, empty dashboard dead end after the tour. Great for the activation/time-to-value measurement narrative.

teardownTargets.product: An analytics or dashboard product's empty state and first-value path (e.g. Amplitude/Mixpanel or a newer AI analytics tool)
teardownTargets.why: Empty state is often a 'No data' wall rather than a first lesson; the aha (first insight) sits behind a data-connection setup step, blowing the time-to-value budget. Shows setup-latency and empty-state-as-onboarding fixes concretely.

teardownTargets.product: A no-code/AI builder success-to-next-step flow (e.g. an AI app/website builder's 'your app is ready' screen)
teardownTargets.why: Terminal success screen and missing next-loop routing: the build completes, then the user is stranded with no obvious path to publish/iterate/share. Demonstrates state+next-action pairing and progressive activation ladder failures.

subNodes.label: The loop is the unit of design, not the screen
subNodes.oneLiner: A task is a closed cycle (intent to action to feedback to interpretation to next intent), not a page you land on.
subNodes.body: Norman's seven-stage action cycle says every interaction spans two gulfs: the Gulf of Execution (can I act toward my goal?) and the Gulf of Evaluation (did it work, and what now?). Designers ship the execution side and starve the evaluation side, so the loop never closes. In AI/crypto this is fatal: an agent that acts but doesn't legibly report state, or a transaction that broadcasts but gives no confirmation, reads as untrustworthy precisely because the evaluation half is missing.

subNodes.label: Compelling context: users want to be badass, not to use your tool
subNodes.oneLiner: People don't hire the product to use features; they hire it to make progress they can feel.
subNodes.body: Kathy Sierra's reframe: the user's real goal lives outside your UI (ship the report, close the incident, move the funds safely). Feature-based products optimize tool mastery; task-based products optimize user capability. For a Sam-type founder, this is the difference between 'powerful but I feel stupid' (leaks users) and 'I did the thing and I feel competent' (retains). Trust is a byproduct of felt competence.

subNodes.label: JTBD Forces of Progress govern whether the loop even starts
subNodes.oneLiner: Switching is push + pull vs. anxiety + habit; anxiety is the force interface design can most directly lower.
subNodes.body: Moesta/Christensen: two forces drive adoption (push from the old pain, pull toward the new outcome) and two block it (anxiety of the new, habit of the present). Onboarding is not decoration; it is anxiety-reduction engineering. AI ('will it hallucinate and I get blamed?') and crypto ('will I lose my funds forever?') are anxiety-dominant categories, so the loop's first turn must retire specific fears, not just show features.

subNodes.label: Activation = the first closed loop that predicts retention
subNodes.oneLiner: Activation is the earliest behavioral event statistically correlated with a flattening retention curve, not a signup or a tour finish.
subNodes.body: The aha moment is emotional and qualitative; the activation event is the measurable proxy for it (Facebook's '7 friends in 10 days', Slack's '2,000 messages sent'). If your activation metric doesn't correlate with a retention curve that flattens to a non-zero floor, you've picked a vanity milestone. This is the single most load-bearing measurement decision in SaaS growth.

subNodes.label: Time-to-value is a latency budget, and you can spend it wrong
subNodes.oneLiner: Every step between signup and first value is latency; onboarding is a budget you allocate, not a checklist you complete.
subNodes.body: Self-serve B2B benchmarks: under 5 min is excellent, 20-60 min bleeds signups. Setup work (invite team, connect data, configure) is latency the user pays before any payoff. The senior move is to defer or fake setup (Basecamp's pre-populated sample projects) so the first value moment lands before the anxiety budget runs out.

subNodes.label: Nouns before verbs: structure the system, then choreograph the tasks
subNodes.oneLiner: Define the objects and their relationships (OOUX) first; task flows are the verbs you attach to a stable noun-graph.
subNodes.body: Sophia Prater's OOUX: teams that slice only by task flow ship disjointed, cobbled-together UIs because there's no consistent object model underneath. Developers already think object-orientedly, so a designer who models objects/attributes/relationships/CTAs speaks the codebase's language. The synthesis for this cluster: object-oriented IA for navigation stability, task-based loops for the journey through it. Neither alone is enough.

subNodes.label: Match friction to stakes (calibrated trust)
subNodes.oneLiner: Confirmation cost should scale with reversibility and blast radius, not be uniform across the app.
subNodes.body: For agentic and crypto products, both over-trust and under-trust are failures. Silent auto-execution on trivial actions, hard checkpoints before irreversible/costly ones. A UI that presents an AI agent as infallible (smooth, confident, zero visible uncertainty) makes operators stop checking, which is more dangerous than visible uncertainty. Trust comes from cheap, always-available control (pause, correct, undo), not from hiding the machinery.

subNodes.label: Straight-line / Bowling Alley onboarding
subNodes.oneLiner: When there is one dominant first job and multiple ways to wander off it. Put the user on a single line to first value; use 'bumpers' (product nudges + human/lifecycle messages) to catch the gutters (drop-off points). Strip every step that isn't on the critical path to the aha event.
subNodes.body: Example: Casey Winters / ProductLed 'Bowling Alley Framework'; Duolingo's first-lesson-before-signup; Superhuman's concierge onboarding as a human bumper.

subNodes.label: Empty state as the first lesson (teaching zero-state)
subNodes.oneLiner: Any container that starts empty (dashboard, inbox, workspace). Use the blank slate to sell the benefit and demonstrate the completed job, not to apologize for emptiness.
subNodes.body: Example: Basecamp pre-populating sample projects so users see the shape of the filled state; a good empty state shows one primary CTA that starts the core loop plus a preview of the 'after'.

subNodes.label: Do-it-for-me first turn (skip setup, borrow data)
subNodes.oneLiner: When required setup (connect data source, invite team, configure) sits between signup and value. Fake or defer it: sample data, templates, social/email login instead of seed phrases.
subNodes.body: Example: Web3 embedded wallets (email/social login, seed phrase managed in background) report 30-40% higher onboarding completion vs. external-wallet seed-phrase flows.

subNodes.label: Editable plan / plan-then-execute for agents
subNodes.oneLiner: AI agent that will take multi-step, consequential action. Show the plan as an editable artifact before execution; let the user amend the next steps. This closes the execution gulf (I can steer) and the evaluation gulf (I can see intent).
subNodes.body: Example: Coding agents' plan-search-modify-verify cycle; a validation feed / persistent action log that operators cite as the reason they trust delegation.

subNodes.label: Progressive activation ladder (setup -> aha -> habit)
subNodes.oneLiner: When a single activation event isn't enough to predict retention. Instrument three ordered milestones (Setup moment, Aha moment, Habit moment) and design a distinct loop for each.
subNodes.body: Example: Amplitude's 4-stage model (signed up, setup, aha, habit); measure completion of each as its own funnel step and tie the habit moment to your North Star.

subNodes.label: State + next-action pairing (close the loop in the UI)
subNodes.oneLiner: Every action's result view. Never show a terminal 'success' with no onward path. Pair confirmation with the highest-probability next job so the loop feeds the next loop.
subNodes.body: Example: After 'invoice sent': show status + 'send reminder in 7 days' / 'create next invoice'. Prevents the dead-end where a completed task strands the user.

subNodes.label: Feature-based navigation that hides the job
subNodes.oneLiner: Menus named after internal modules/features force the user to reverse-engineer which feature performs their task. The job is spread across 4 tabs with no path between them. Users conclude the product 'can't do' something it can do, and leak. Common in AI tools that expose model/config surface area instead of outcomes.

subNodes.label: The loop that never closes (fire-and-forget)
subNodes.oneLiner: Action succeeds but the system gives no legible state change or next step. In agents: the agent acts and returns to an idle prompt with no record of what changed. In crypto: transaction broadcasts, spinner spins, no confirmation. The Gulf of Evaluation stays open, so the user can't tell success from failure and stops trusting the system.

subNodes.label: Onboarding-as-tour (feature carousel)
subNodes.oneLiner: A modal tooltip tour narrates features before the user has done anything meaningful. It inflates a vanity 'onboarding completion' metric while activation stays flat, because narrated features don't produce felt progress. Users click through to dismiss it, then face an empty screen with no idea what to do.

subNodes.label: Terminal success screen / dead end
subNodes.oneLiner: 'You're all set!' with a single 'Done' button drops the user back to a blank dashboard. The completed task doesn't hand off to the next job, so the second loop never starts, activation stalls at one action, and the retention curve decays.

subNodes.label: Uniform confirmation friction
subNodes.oneLiner: Same confirm dialog on trivial and catastrophic actions trains users to click through everything, so the one confirmation that mattered (irreversible transfer, destructive agent action) gets dismissed reflexively. Friction must scale with blast radius.

subNodes.label: Re-briefing the agent every time (no state carried in the loop)
subNodes.oneLiner: The fastest way to make an agentic product feel broken: the human re-explains context on every interaction because corrections aren't internalized. Feedback loops that collect input then do nothing kill trust faster than a runaway agent.

subNodes.label: Task-flow-only design with no object model
subNodes.oneLiner: Slicing the product only by user stories/flows (verbs) with no shared noun model yields inconsistent entities across screens, orphaned records, and navigation that can't scale. It also breaks the designer-developer shared language, since engineers model objects.

subNodes.label: The evaluation half of the loop is silently missing: the action fires ...
subNodes.oneLiner: The evaluation half of the loop is silently missing: the action fires (POST succeeds, tx broadcasts, agent runs) but there is no state read-back in the UI. A code-reading designer spots that the success handler navigates or toasts but never re-fetches/renders the new object state, so the user can't confirm the outcome. This is the #1 source of 'feels untrustworthy'.

subNodes.label: Optimistic UI lies during failure: the interface shows success immedia...
subNodes.oneLiner: Optimistic UI lies during failure: the interface shows success immediately, but the async job later fails with no rollback and no error surface. Users believe a thing happened that didn't. Only visible by reading the error path, not the happy path.

subNodes.label: Activation metric measures the wrong event: the tracked 'activation' f...
subNodes.oneLiner: Activation metric measures the wrong event: the tracked 'activation' fires on a tour-complete or a signup callback, not on a value-producing action, so it correlates with nothing. Reading the analytics instrumentation reveals the event is bound to a UI mount, not a domain event.

subNodes.label: Dead ends created by missing next-state routing: the success view has ...
subNodes.oneLiner: Dead ends created by missing next-state routing: the success view has no onward CTA in the component; the router returns to a generic dashboard. The loop closes but doesn't feed the next loop. Invisible in static mockups, obvious in the flow.

subNodes.label: Setup latency hidden in required fields and blocking API calls: onboar...
subNodes.oneLiner: Setup latency hidden in required fields and blocking API calls: onboarding form gates first value behind a data connection or team invite that the code makes synchronous/required. The time-to-value budget is blown before the user does anything meaningful.

subNodes.label: Feature-based IA baked into the route structure: routes/nav are genera...
subNodes.oneLiner: Feature-based IA baked into the route structure: routes/nav are generated from module names or permission scopes, so the job is fragmented across tabs by accident of code organization, not by user intent.

subNodes.label: Confirmation friction not tied to reversibility: reading the code show...
subNodes.oneLiner: Confirmation friction not tied to reversibility: reading the code shows a single generic Confirm component used everywhere, including irreversible actions, so the destructive path has the same weight as the trivial one.

subNodes.label: Agent action logs exist in the backend but aren't surfaced: the state ...
subNodes.oneLiner: Agent action logs exist in the backend but aren't surfaced: the state that would close the evaluation gulf (what the agent did, why) is logged server-side but never rendered, so trust can't form even though the data exists.

subNodes.label: Empty states hard-coded as 'No data' with no CTA: the zero-state compo...
subNodes.oneLiner: Empty states hard-coded as 'No data' with no CTA: the zero-state component is a placeholder string, not an onboarding surface, so first-run users hit a wall the moment the tour ends.

subNodes.label: Retention curve never flattens but the team celebrates activation: act...
subNodes.oneLiner: Retention curve never flattens but the team celebrates activation: activation is up while the cohort curve decays to zero, meaning the activation event isn't the real aha. Only visible by joining activation instrumentation to cohort retention, which most dashboards don't do.

topics.title: Deceptive Patterns & Trust

methods.method: Amended cognitive walkthrough for deception (NN/g)
methods.measures: Whether a flow can cause users to spend/share more than intended, misinterpret choices, or miss options. Run the walkthrough asking the deception-specific questions (Is each choice factually correct? Could a choice be missed because it's obscured? Is the exchange fair?). Catches MILD patterns that usability tests miss because users don't complain about them.

methods.method: Intention-vs-outcome / task-comparison audit
methods.measures: Divergence between what the user intended and what the interface produced. Compare the stated goal ('cancel my subscription') to the actual number of steps, dead-ends, and off-ramps. Quantify entry-step count vs exit-step count as a hard asymmetry metric.

methods.method: Trust in Automated Systems Scale (Jian, Bisantz & Drury 2000) + validated 2-factor trust/distrust variants
methods.measures: Self-reported trust as a numeric construct, 12 items. Note the documented positive-bias critique (Gutzwiller et al. 2019) and the two-factor (trust vs. distrust) refinement, so treat it as directional. Use pre/post a design change to detect movement, not as an absolute.

methods.method: Randomized dark-pattern A/B with effect-size reporting (Luguri & Strahilevitz method)
methods.measures: Causal effect of a specific pattern on acceptance. Their large study found aggressive dark patterns nearly quadrupled acceptance and even mild ones roughly doubled it, with disproportionate impact on lower-education users. As a designer, run the inverse: measure how much a de-darkened variant recovers honest choice.

methods.method: Consent/decision A/B on choice architecture (Nouwens et al. method)
methods.measures: How placement and granularity of options change decisions: removing opt-out from the first layer raised consent 22-23pp; more granular first-layer controls dropped it 8-20pp. Directly quantifies the coercive value of asymmetry.

methods.method: Hesitation-time & drop-off instrumentation at trust moments
methods.measures: Time-to-action, rage-clicks, form-abandonment, and scroll/hover dwell precisely at the seed-phrase screen, first-deposit, connect-wallet, payment, and permission prompts. Spikes in hesitation or drop-off localize WHERE trust breaks. Pair session replay (heatmaps, replays) with funnel drop-off at those specific steps rather than aggregate funnel numbers.

methods.method: Automated dark-pattern detection / DOM & network crawl
methods.measures: Programmatic detection of pre-ticked boxes, reject-button depth, injected social-proof scripts, countdown-timer reset behavior. Mathur used ML classification over crawled pages; a designer can do a lighter version with DevTools/Playwright to flag asymmetry in markup and third-party manipulation widgets.

methods.method: Sludge audit (Sunstein)
methods.measures: Total friction cost (time, steps, documents, waits) on beneficial-to-user actions vs. beneficial-to-business actions. Produces a defensible asymmetry ledger you can put in a teardown.

tactics: Lead teardowns with the 5-attribute lens, not the pattern name. Instead of 'this is confirmshaming,' say 'this is a Covert emotional-manipulation attribute that inflates conversion by X but is now cited in DSA Art. 25.' Naming the mechanism + the regulation is what makes a founder ('Sam') take it seriously.

Convert every trust claim into an ABI signal placed at the hesitation moment. For each Ability/Benevolence/Integrity claim, answer: is it Prominent at the decision point, and is it Interpreted correctly by THIS user segment (crypto-native vs. normie)? Move signals from the footer to the confirm sheet.

Instrument the asymmetry, then show the number. 'Signing up is 2 clicks; cancelling is 6 clicks and a phone call' is more persuasive to a founder than any qualitative critique, and it maps directly to FTC/DSA exposure.

For AI products, design for calibrated reliance: surface per-output confidence, sources, and a cheap way to verify, and add friction proportional to irreversibility. Explicitly argue against 'make it sound more confident' by citing the explainability paradox and automation-bias research.

For crypto, treat the confirmation sheet as the entire product. Decode calldata to human-readable asset deltas, cap approvals by default, simulate outcomes, flag unlimited approvals and unknown contracts. The trust battle is won or lost in that one modal.

Reframe 'friction is bad' for the founder: distinguish good friction (confirmation before irreversible/high-consequence acts = trust infrastructure) from sludge (friction on the user's own exit). Optimize sludge to zero; keep consequence-friction.

Build a reusable 'trust-leak audit' artifact: for a target product, map each screen to (a) which of the 5 attributes it triggers, (b) which ABI signal is missing or mis-placed, (c) the measurable metric (step asymmetry, hesitation, drop-off), (d) the regulation it brushes against. That format is publishable as a teardown and sellable as a service.

Cite the regulation as leverage, not decoration. GDPR (consent asymmetry), CCPA/CPRA (opt-out symmetry), FTC click-to-cancel + the Amazon Prime case, DSA Art. 25 (Meta/Temu/Shein probes). Founders respond to 'this is now an enforcement target' faster than to 'this is unethical.'

resources.title: Deceptive Patterns: Exposing the Tricks Tech Companies Use to Control You
resources.why: The canonical book by the person who coined 'dark pattern' in 2010. Chapters 13-21 lay out the Mathur et al. taxonomy category-by-category; also covers harms and enforcement. The single best foundation text and the free web version at deceptive.design/book is fully readable.

resources.title: Dark Patterns at Scale: Findings from a Crawl of 11K Shopping Websites
resources.source: Mathur, Acar, Friedman, Lucherini, Mayer, Chetty, Narayanan (ACM CSCW 2019)
resources.why: The load-bearing empirical paper: 1,818 dark-pattern instances, 15 types, 7 categories, on ~11.1% of sites, plus 22 turnkey third-party providers named. This is the data you cite in any teardown. arXiv 1907.07032.

resources.title: What Makes a Dark Pattern... Dark? Design Attributes, Normative Considerations, and Measurement Methods
resources.source: Arunesh Mathur, Jonathan Mayer, Mihir Kshirsagar (CHI 2021)
resources.why: Defines the 5 attributes (asymmetric, covert, deceptive, information-hiding, restrictive) that are THE systems-level lens for auditing any UI, and surveys how to measure darkness. arXiv 2101.04843. More useful for an advanced designer than the pattern catalog.

resources.title: The Dark (Patterns) Side of UX Design
resources.source: Colin M. Gray, Kou, Battles, Hoggatt, Toombs (CHI 2018)
resources.why: The practitioner-facing taxonomy: Nagging, Obstruction, Sneaking, Interface Interference, Forced Action. Framed around how UX designers themselves reason about these, which makes it the right vocabulary for belief-shift posts aimed at product teams.

resources.title: Dark Patterns after the GDPR: Scraping Consent Pop-ups and Demonstrating their Influence
resources.why: The quantified proof that choice architecture coerces: <12% of CMPs GDPR-compliant; removing opt-out from layer one lifted consent 22-23pp. Gives you hard numbers for the 'asymmetry is measurable' argument.

resources.title: Shining a Light on Dark Patterns
resources.source: Jamie Luguri & Lior Jacob Strahilevitz (Journal of Legal Analysis, 2021)
resources.why: Large randomized experiment establishing effect sizes: aggressive dark patterns ~quadrupled and mild ones ~doubled acceptance, hitting lower-education users hardest. The go-to citation for 'this actually changes behavior, and it's regressive.'

resources.title: Prominence-Interpretation Theory + Stanford Guidelines for Web Credibility
resources.source: B.J. Fogg, Stanford Persuasive Technology Lab (2002-2003)
resources.why: The foundational trust-design theory: credibility = Prominence x Interpretation, modulated by involvement/task/experience. The Stanford Guidelines (10 items) are the original credibility checklist. Explains why real trust signals fail when mis-placed.

resources.title: An Integrative Model of Organizational Trust
resources.source: Roger Mayer, James Davis, F. David Schoorman (Academy of Management Review, 1995)
resources.why: The Ability-Benevolence-Integrity model and the trust-vs-trustworthiness + vulnerability distinction. The ethical backbone for 'evidence real trustworthiness, don't manufacture trust' and directly applicable to high-vulnerability crypto/AI contexts.

resources.title: Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance
resources.source: John D. Lee & Katrina A. See (Human Factors, 2004)
resources.why: Defines trust in automation and the overtrust/undertrust -> misuse/disuse framework and calibration. The canonical lens for AI product trust; the intellectual counter to 'make the AI sound more confident.'

resources.title: Foundations for an Empirically Determined Scale of Trust in Automated Systems
resources.source: Jian, Bisantz & Drury (International Journal of Cognitive Ergonomics, 2000)
resources.why: The 12-item trust-in-automation survey used in 100+ studies; the standard instrument for measuring trust before/after a design change. Note the positive-bias critique (Gutzwiller et al. 2019) and two-factor refinement when you use it.

resources.title: Bringing Dark Patterns to Light (FTC Staff Report)
resources.source: US Federal Trade Commission, Bureau of Consumer Protection (Sept 2022)
resources.why: Regulator's own taxonomy and enforcement posture across false-belief, unauthorized-charge, and privacy-subverting patterns. Pair with the Amazon Prime 'Iliad' cancellation case and click-to-cancel rule. This is the leverage language for founders.

resources.title: deceptive.design (Hall of Shame + pattern library) and Colin Gray's darkpatterns.uxp2.com corpus
resources.why: Living catalogs of real, screenshotted patterns in the wild, updated with new examples and regulation. Best source for fresh, dated teardown material and for tracking who's currently being caught.

teardownTargets.product: A major non-custodial wallet transaction-confirmation flow (e.g., MetaMask token-approval / signature request; contrast with Rabby)
teardownTargets.why: The clearest live case of Information-Hiding + Covert + irreversibility. Tear down the confirm sheet: does it decode calldata to asset deltas, default to capped vs unlimited approval, flag unknown contracts, and simulate the outcome? MetaMask historically showed opaque approvals; Rabby popularized pre-tx simulation and risk scanning. Perfect for a 'blind signing is a trust bug, not a UX detail' post.

teardownTargets.product: A centralized crypto exchange onboarding + withdrawal path (e.g., Coinbase or Binance)  -  entry vs. exit asymmetry
teardownTargets.why: Instrument sign-up/deposit step count against KYC-gated withdrawal/off-ramp step count and holds. Surfaces Obstruction/sludge and the trust-destroying gap between 'get money in' friction and 'get money out' friction. Ties to FTC/DSA enforcement themes.

teardownTargets.product: A generative-AI answer or agent UI (e.g., an LLM chat product or an AI 'agent' that takes actions)
teardownTargets.why: Audit for manufactured confidence: uniform authoritative tone, missing per-output confidence, dropped uncertainty from the API, and irreversible actions taken without a preview/undo. Apply Lee & See calibration + the explainability paradox. Strong 'invisible problem' material a code-reading designer can prove by diffing API response vs. rendered output.

teardownTargets.product: A subscription SaaS cancellation flow (e.g., a streaming or productivity tool) vs. its checkout
teardownTargets.why: Classic roach-motel / sludge teardown with hard metrics (entry clicks vs exit clicks, retention-offer interstitials, confirmshaming on the cancel button). Directly maps to FTC click-to-cancel and the Amazon Prime case, so the post carries regulatory weight.

teardownTargets.product: A cookie/consent or notification-permission banner on a high-traffic AI/SaaS site (any CMP-driven banner)
teardownTargets.why: Inspect the DOM: reject-button depth, pre-ticked boxes, accept/reject widget-hierarchy asymmetry, granularity placement. Nouwens' method makes this quantifiable and GDPR/CPRA-testable  -  a compact teardown that shows the value of reading markup, not pixels.

subNodes.label: Mathur's 5 attributes (the mechanism lens, not the pattern-name lens)
subNodes.oneLiner: A pattern is 'dark' by HOW it distorts choice: it's Asymmetric (unequal option prominence), Covert (hidden influence mechanism), Deceptive (induces false belief), Information-Hiding (delays/obscures needed info), or Restrictive (removes options).
subNodes.body: This is the load-bearing model for a code-reading designer. Pattern names (confirmshaming, roach motel) are surface labels; the 5 attributes are the underlying operators. You can audit ANY AI/crypto/SaaS screen by asking which of the 5 it triggers, even for patterns nobody has named yet (e.g. an LLM confidently omitting its uncertainty = Information-Hiding + Covert). Mathur et al. also split these into 'modifies the decision space' (asymmetric/restrictive/covert) vs 'manipulates the information flow' (deceptive/hiding), which maps cleanly to front-end structure vs. copy/state.

subNodes.label: Prominence x Interpretation (Fogg): credibility is a two-step perceptual event
subNodes.oneLiner: Users form a credibility judgment only when an element is (1) Prominent enough to be noticed AND (2) Interpreted as good/bad; miss either step and the signal does nothing.
subNodes.body: Explains why crypto/AI products that ARE trustworthy still 'read as untrustworthy': their trust signals (audits, security badges, provenance) exist but aren't prominent at the decision moment, or are interpreted through the wrong frame. It reframes trust work as placement + framing, not just adding more badges. Prominence is modulated by user involvement, task, and experience, so a novice and a whale read the same screen differently.

subNodes.label: Trust vs. trustworthiness (Mayer-Davis-Schoorman): Ability + Benevolence + Integrity
subNodes.oneLiner: Trust is the willingness to be vulnerable; trustworthiness is the target's actual Ability, Benevolence, and Integrity. Design can only honestly move trust by evidencing the three; anything else is manufacturing trust the system hasn't earned.
subNodes.body: Gives an ethical dividing line: persuasion evidences real ABI, deception fakes it. For AI/crypto where the user is maximally vulnerable (irreversible txns, opaque model outputs), the model tells you WHICH signal to show: Ability (audits, benchmarks, uptime), Benevolence (this-costs-you-X disclosures, easy exits), Integrity (consistent behavior, honest error states).

subNodes.label: Trust calibration & appropriate reliance (Lee & See): the goal is not MORE trust
subNodes.oneLiner: The objective is trust matched to actual capability: overtrust causes misuse (blindly signing, accepting a hallucination), undertrust causes disuse (abandoning a good product). Design for the right amount, not the maximum.
subNodes.body: Directly hits AI/crypto. Confident explanations can INCREASE overreliance by reducing critical reflection (the explainability paradox). A trust-first designer surfaces uncertainty, confidence, and reversibility so reliance tracks reality. This is the intellectual counter to 'just make it feel more confident.'

subNodes.label: Asymmetry of consequences: trust is destroyed faster than built, and irreversibility amplifies it
subNodes.oneLiner: Trust accrues linearly through consistent positive interactions but collapses on a single violation; when the action is irreversible (on-chain transfer, deleted data, sent funds) the collapse is total and permanent.
subNodes.body: In crypto a single blind-signed malicious approval = total loss = permanent distrust of the wallet, not just the dApp. In AI, one confidently-wrong output on a high-stakes task poisons reliance on all future outputs. This is why reversibility, undo, simulation/preview, and confirmation friction are trust infrastructure, not UX friction to be optimized away.

subNodes.label: Sludge: dark patterns' quiet twin (Thaler/Sunstein)
subNodes.oneLiner: Sludge is friction deliberately placed to discourage an action in the user's interest (cancel, opt-out, withdraw) while the beneficial-to-business action stays frictionless. It's the Obstruction/Restrictive attribute expressed as process, not screen.
subNodes.body: The invisible half of trust leak. A code-reading designer can literally count clicks/steps/round-trips on the cancel or withdraw flow vs. the sign-up or deposit flow. Asymmetry in that count IS the dark pattern, even when every individual screen looks clean. Regulators (FTC click-to-cancel, DSA) now treat this asymmetry as the violation.

subNodes.label: Reversibility-first / preview-then-commit
subNodes.oneLiner: Any irreversible or high-consequence action: crypto signing, fund transfer, model action in an agent, bulk delete, plan downgrade. Simulate the outcome ('you will send 10 USDC, receive nothing, grant unlimited approval to 0xABC') in human-readable terms BEFORE the commit, and add an undo window where physically possible.
subNodes.body: Example: Rabby wallet's pre-transaction simulation and risk scanning; token-approval editors that let you cap allowance instead of unlimited. The trust move is decoding raw calldata into asset-change deltas at the confirmation moment.

subNodes.label: Symmetric exits (anti-roach-motel)
subNodes.oneLiner: Whenever you design a sign-up, subscribe, connect-wallet, or grant-permission flow. Rule: the exit path must have equal-or-fewer steps and equal prominence to the entry path. Cancel online if you subscribed online.
subNodes.body: Example: FTC 'click-to-cancel' logic and the Amazon Prime 'Iliad' cancellation case. As a designer, instrument step-count parity: entry_steps must be >= exit_steps.

subNodes.label: Honest uncertainty surfacing (calibrated confidence)
subNodes.oneLiner: AI outputs, risk scores, price estimates, fraud flags. Show confidence per-instance, cite sources, and make low-confidence visibly different from high-confidence. Presenting case-by-case confidence measurably reduced automation bias in pilot studies.
subNodes.body: Example: Perplexity-style inline citations; showing 'this is an estimate, range $X-$Y' rather than a single false-precision number. The anti-goal is a uniformly confident tone that flattens real uncertainty.

subNodes.label: Provenance & receipts (Integrity evidence)
subNodes.oneLiner: Crypto (on-chain verifiability, contract source, audit links placed AT the action), AI (why did the model do this, what data), SaaS (audit logs, change history). Make the system's past behavior inspectable at the moment trust is required.
subNodes.body: Example: Etherscan 'verified contract' green check surfaced inside the wallet confirm sheet, not buried on a block explorer the user must leave to find.

subNodes.label: Just-in-time, framed trust signals (Prominence x Interpretation applied)
subNodes.oneLiner: At the specific hesitation moment (payment, seed-phrase, first deposit, connect). Place the credibility signal where it will be noticed AND frame it so it's interpreted correctly (e.g., 'SOC 2 audited' means little to a crypto-native; 'non-custodial, we never hold your keys' lands).
subNodes.body: Example: Stripe's checkout showing the lock + 'Powered by Stripe' at the card field, not in a footer. Contrast with a security badge in the footer that is prominent-to-nobody at decision time.

subNodes.label: Neutral defaults + symmetric choice architecture
subNodes.oneLiner: Cookie/consent, notification opt-ins, data-sharing, plan selection. Accept and Reject must be the same widget type, same hierarchy, same click-cost. No pre-ticked boxes.
subNodes.body: Example: GDPR-compliant consent per Nouwens et al.: reject-all on the first layer with equal prominence to accept-all. This is measurable and enforceable.

subNodes.label: Blind signing / opaque confirmation (crypto)
subNodes.oneLiner: The wallet shows 'Approve 10 USDC' while the actual calldata grants unlimited spend or transfers an NFT. It's Information-Hiding + Covert + irreversible = the single most trust-destroying pattern in web3. Fails because the user cannot consent to what they cannot read; one exploit and the wallet brand is dead.

subNodes.label: Confirmshaming
subNodes.oneLiner: The decline option is worded to shame ('No, I don't want to save money'). It's a Covert emotional-manipulation pattern. Short-term conversion lift, long-term brand contempt; users screenshot and post these. Explicitly cited by FTC and DSA.

subNodes.label: Fake/false urgency & scarcity (countdown timers, 'only 2 left', activity notifications)
subNodes.oneLiner: Mathur found these are frequently non-genuine and often sold as turnkey third-party widgets (Fomo, Beeketing, etc.). Deceptive if the timer resets or the stock number is fabricated. In AI/SaaS it shows up as fake 'X people signed up in the last hour.' Erodes Integrity the moment a user reloads and sees the timer reset.

subNodes.label: Manufactured confidence in AI outputs
subNodes.oneLiner: Uniformly authoritative tone with no uncertainty, no sources, no confidence signal. Drives overtrust/automation bias; users accept hallucinations on high-stakes tasks. The explainability paradox: a slick explanation can make a wrong answer MORE trusted. Catastrophic when the output is acted on irreversibly.

subNodes.label: Roach motel / hard-to-cancel (Obstruction)
subNodes.oneLiner: Easy to subscribe online, must phone/email to cancel. Now explicitly illegal under FTC click-to-cancel logic and DSA Art. 25. The asymmetry is trivially measurable (entry steps vs exit steps) and is a lawsuit magnet.

subNodes.label: Consent-string dark patterns (interface interference in cookie/permission banners)
subNodes.oneLiner: Reject buried a layer deep, pre-ticked boxes, accept visually dominant. Nouwens et al.: <12% of scraped CMPs were GDPR-compliant; removing reject from the first page lifted consent 22-23pp. It's a legally-quantified violation, and users increasingly recognize and resent it.

subNodes.label: Trust-badge theater
subNodes.oneLiner: Piling security/audit/press logos that are either unverifiable, irrelevant to the user's mental model, or placed where nobody looks. Fails Prominence-Interpretation on both axes and, worse, sophisticated users read badge density itself as a distrust signal (protesting too much).

subNodes.label: Entry/exit step asymmetry that no single screenshot reveals. Only by w...
subNodes.oneLiner: Entry/exit step asymmetry that no single screenshot reveals. Only by walking (or reading the router/state machine of) the full cancel/withdraw/opt-out flow versus the sign-up/deposit flow do you see the Obstruction. A code-reading designer counts routes, API round-trips, and required fields on each path.

subNodes.label: Third-party manipulation widgets injected via <script>. Fake 'social p...
subNodes.oneLiner: Third-party manipulation widgets injected via <script>. Fake 'social proof' and 'urgency' notifications (Fomo, Beeketing, Proof, Yieldify) are drop-in JS. Reading the network tab / DOM reveals the activity messages are client-side fabrications with randomized names, not real events. Invisible to anyone who only looks at the rendered UI.

subNodes.label: Consent asymmetry encoded in the DOM, not the visuals. Accept and Reje...
subNodes.oneLiner: Consent asymmetry encoded in the DOM, not the visuals. Accept and Reject may look similar but sit at different levels of the hierarchy, fire different event handlers, or Reject is a link while Accept is a button. Inspecting the markup exposes the asymmetry that pixel-inspection misses. Also: pre-ticked boxes whose 'checked' state is set in JS after paint.

subNodes.label: Raw calldata vs. displayed intent divergence (crypto). The wallet's co...
subNodes.oneLiner: Raw calldata vs. displayed intent divergence (crypto). The wallet's confirmation copy is a human-authored string; the actual signed payload is the hex. A designer who reads the transaction object sees when 'Approve 10 USDC' actually encodes an unlimited approval or a setApprovalForAll. The gap between rendered text and signed bytes is the whole attack surface.

subNodes.label: False precision and hidden uncertainty in AI/data UIs. A model outputs...
subNodes.oneLiner: False precision and hidden uncertainty in AI/data UIs. A model outputs a single confident number/answer; the underlying API returns a confidence score, token logprobs, or a range that the UI silently discards. The dropped uncertainty is an Information-Hiding pattern the designer can catch by diffing the API response against what's rendered.

subNodes.label: Optimistic UI that lies about irreversible state. Front-ends show 'Sen...
subNodes.oneLiner: Optimistic UI that lies about irreversible state. Front-ends show 'Sent!' / 'Saved!' on optimistic update before on-chain confirmation or server ack. If it silently fails or reverts, the user's trust model and reality diverge. Reading the state-management (optimistic vs. confirmed) reveals where the UI is writing checks the backend hasn't cashed.

subNodes.label: Default-object smuggling. Pre-selected expensive plan, pre-added add-o...
subNodes.oneLiner: Default-object smuggling. Pre-selected expensive plan, pre-added add-on, or a default 'share my data: on' set in the initial state/reducer rather than shown as a checked box. The default lives in code/config, not visibly in the UI, so it reads as neutral while steering asymmetrically.

topics.title: Buying Psychology

methods.method: Funnel drop-off analysis segmented by step AND user cohort
methods.measures: Where and for whom the leak happens. Baymard-style step-level abandonment; the discipline is to re-measure the WHOLE funnel after any fix, because a change that lifts step 3 often pushes the drop to step 5.

methods.method: Session replay filtered by friction signals (rage clicks, thrashing, dead clicks, error events)
methods.measures: The qualitative 'why' behind a drop step. Standard practice: pull 10-20 replays of users who exited at the target step, or trial users stuck >5 min on one onboarding step, before theorizing a cause.

methods.method: Mouse-cursor tracking for hesitation kinematics
methods.measures: Decision uncertainty at a specific control. Established measures (Freeman & Ambady's MouseTracker; Hehman/Stolier/Freeman analytics): trajectory deviation/curvature toward the rejected option, velocity, direction reversals ('x-flips'), sample entropy, and hover count (cursor stationary >500ms) as an operational hesitation marker. Distinguishes 'confused' from 'reconsidering'.

methods.method: Dwell time / time-on-step as a System-1 vs System-2 proxy
methods.measures: Whether users are actually reading the high-stakes confirmation. Very low dwell on a critical confirm screen is a red flag for blind-clicking; very high dwell signals ambiguity/comprehension failure. Interpret against the reversibility of the step.

methods.method: Exit-intent and post-abandon surveys (one question, triggered by funnel behavior)
methods.measures: Self-reported reason at the moment of leaving. Best paired with the quantitative drop step so you know exactly which screen the answer refers to; keeps you from mis-attributing a trust problem to a price problem.

methods.method: Drift-diffusion / evidence-accumulation modeling of choice + RT
methods.measures: Decomposes a hesitation into its causes: drift rate (quality of evidence the UI provides), boundary (how much certainty the user demands, i.e. their caution), and non-decision time. Lets you tell apart 'the UI gives weak evidence' from 'this is inherently a scary irreversible choice' - different fixes.

methods.method: Trust-calibration measurement for AI actions (reliance vs. actual accuracy)
methods.measures: Over-reliance and under-reliance. Track how often users accept vs. override the agent, cross-referenced with whether the agent was actually right; the target is appropriate reliance, not a high accept rate. Miscalibration (accepting wrong actions, overriding right ones) is the KPI, not raw acceptance.

methods.method: Controlled A/B on friction placement, not just friction removal
methods.measures: Whether a deliberate speed bump at an irreversible step reduces regret/reversal/support tickets without materially hurting completion. The honest test: does added friction lower error/chargeback/failed-tx rates? Measure regret proxies (reversals, disputes, immediate undo, rage), not only conversion.

tactics: Weight friction by reversibility, explicitly. Introduce a riskTier/reversible variable that threads through your confirm components so a one-tap confirm and a typed-SEND confirm are the same component in different states. This is a systems move a code-reading designer can actually ship and defend to engineers.

Convert ambiguity into bounded risk at every high-stakes step: state the exact outcome, the counterparty, the scope, and the worst case in plain language. 'This lets X spend up to 50 USDC' beats any reassurance copy. Adopt/borrow the ERC-7730 clear-signing pattern even outside crypto (e.g., for AI agent action previews).
Kill drip pricing: surface the full landed cost (gas/spread/fees) at the FIRST screen and hold the anchor. Attack the #1 documented abandonment cause instead of decorating the last step.

Use honest operational transparency at the wait/black-box moments: show the real steps and real sources the AI is touching. Trust the labor illusion, but never fake the labor, it fails the regret test the instant it's discovered.

Design for calibrated, not maximal, trust in AI: surface uncertainty, give a real intervention point (pause/inspect/undo before commit), and default agents to 'ask before acting' with autonomy as an explicit opt-in. This is what makes a founder's product read as trustworthy to sophisticated buyers.

Stage sensitive disclosures by the privacy calculus: order fields by rising sensitivity, justify each scary ask inline with a one-line why + storage note, defer the highest-risk field until after the user has seen value and made a small real commitment.

Apply Cialdini honestly by passing every persuasive mechanism through Eyal's regret test: 'would the user, knowing everything I know, be glad they did this?' Social proof must be real, scarcity must be true, defaults must favor the user's safe option. Honest persuasion and dark patterns use the same levers; the regret test is the line.

Fix ability before motivation (Fogg): at a stalled money/approval step, first cut the cognitive cost (decode, pre-fill, chunk, default) rather than adding hype. Measure completion after the ability fix before touching copy.

Treat error/pending/timeout states as first-class design surfaces, since that is where hesitation actually lives. A legible pending state ('submitted, awaiting confirmation, safe to close') beats a frozen spinner for trust more than any happy-path polish.

Publish the teardown lens as your content edge: 'I read the code before I judge the design' works because most trust failures (blind signing, unlimited approvals, optimistic UI, fake confidence badges) are only visible in the payload, not the pixels.

resources.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
resources.why: The canonical primary source for System 1/2 and (with Tversky) prospect theory and loss aversion. Non-negotiable baseline; read it to cite the mechanisms correctly, then use the newer meta-analyses to avoid over-claiming.

resources.title: Loss Aversion: What Survives of Behavioral Economics' Most Famous Idea (and Gal & Rucker 2018 review)
resources.source: Atticus Li (summary) / David Gal & Derek Rucker, Journal of Consumer Psychology
resources.why: The belief-shift source: loss aversion is context-dependent (field λ≈1.0-1.5, not 2.25). Lets Ashutosh write a credible 'the coefficient you keep citing is wrong' post and stop mis-applying scarcity.

resources.title: Choice Overload: A Conceptual Review and Meta-Analysis
resources.source: Alexander Chernev, Ulf Böckenholt, Joseph Goodman (JCP, 2015); with Scheibehenne, Greifeneder & Todd (2010) meta-analysis
resources.why: The evidence that the jam study doesn't robustly replicate and the moderators that determine when overload is real. Prevents the lazy 'just show fewer options' advice and gives the nuanced version.

resources.title: Risk, Ambiguity, and the Savage Axioms (the Ellsberg Paradox)
resources.source: Daniel Ellsberg, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 1961
resources.why: Primary source for ambiguity aversion, the most underused and highest-leverage model for crypto/AI hesitation (unknown-unknowns vs known risk). Cite the original, not a blog.

resources.title: Tiny Habits / Fogg Behavior Model (B=MAP)
resources.source: BJ Fogg, Stanford Behavior Design Lab
resources.why: Primary source for B=MAP and the 'motivation is the weakest lever / fix ability and prompt' insight. behaviormodel.org is Fogg's own canonical reference for diagramming a specific stalled step.

resources.title: Hooked + the Regret Test / Manipulation Matrix
resources.why: Gives the honest-persuasion line Ashutosh needs: same levers as dark patterns, separated by 'would the user regret this knowing what I know'. Read critically, pair with the FTC report as the counterweight.

resources.title: Bringing Dark Patterns to Light (FTC Staff Report, 2022)
resources.why: Authoritative taxonomy of deceptive design (drip pricing, confirmshaming, steered consent) with enforcement examples. The load-bearing 'what NOT to do' primary source, and increasingly the legal line.

resources.title: The Labor Illusion: How Operational Transparency Increases Perceived Value
resources.source: Ryan W. Buell & Michael I. Norton, Management Science, 2011
