resources.why: Empirical basis for 'friction/visible work can build trust', the counter to 'faster is always better'. Directly applicable to designing honest AI 'showing its work' at the hesitation moment.

resources.title: Clear Signing / ERC-7730 announcement + What You See Is What You Sign
resources.source: Ethereum Foundation (Trillion Dollar Security Initiative), blog + arXiv 'What I Sign Is Not What I See'
resources.why: The single best concrete case study in this cluster: names blind signing as a structural trust flaw (Bybit-scale losses), defines the WYSIWYS fix, and is backed by Ledger/Trezor/MetaMask/WalletConnect. Perfect teardown spine.

resources.title: Mouse-tracking as a window into decision making / MouseTracker
resources.source: Jonathan Freeman & Nalini Ambady (MouseTracker); Freeman review; Hehman, Stolier & Freeman analytics guide
resources.why: The method source for measuring hesitation objectively: trajectory curvature, x-flips, entropy, hover-time >500ms. Turns 'users seem hesitant' into a measurable claim, which is exactly the rigor Ashutosh sells.

resources.title: Baymard Institute checkout & cart abandonment research
resources.why: The definitive quantified source on WHY high-stakes flows leak (drip pricing ~48%, forced account creation, trust/security). Every teardown claim about checkout friction should be anchored to Baymard's numbers.

resources.title: Trust calibration in agentic AI / appropriate reliance (and the Tiered Controllability Framework)
resources.source: Okamura & Yamada (adaptive trust calibration, PMC); designative.info synthesis; TCF
resources.why: The framework for AI-action confirmation UX: design for calibrated reliance (surface uncertainty, real intervention point), and map oversight to risk × reversibility × autonomy. Core to the 'approving an AI action' half of the cluster.

teardownTargets.product: MetaMask transaction / token-approval confirmation screen
teardownTargets.why: The archetypal ambiguity-aversion failure and the archetypal fix in one product: legacy 'Contract Interaction' + unlimited allowance blind-signing vs. the newer decoded/clear-signing and spending-cap UI. Read the calldata vs. what the UI claims; show where WYSIWYS holds and where it breaks. Highest-signal crypto teardown.

teardownTargets.product: Coinbase / Coinbase Wallet 'send crypto' flow (address entry → fee → irreversible confirm)
teardownTargets.why: Consumer-grade crypto where the point-of-no-return, drip-revealed network fees, and optimistic 'sent!' states all live. Test whether friction is reversibility-weighted and whether the final screen forces System-2 re-reading of recipient/amount/fee.

teardownTargets.product: An AI agent action-confirmation surface (e.g. OpenAI Operator / a Claude or Copilot agent's 'about to do X' preview, or Perplexity/Comet-style browsing agent)
teardownTargets.why: The frontier of this cluster: does the UI convert an open-ended agent action into bounded, legible scope? Is 'confidence' real or decorative? Is there a genuine intervention point before commit, or is autonomy the silent default? Trust-calibration teardown gold.

teardownTargets.product: A fintech onboarding/KYC flow (e.g. Robinhood, Wise, Revolut, or Coinbase signup with ID/SSN upload)
teardownTargets.why: Field-by-field privacy-calculus leak: watch where the sensitive ask spikes perceived risk, whether the 'why we need this' is at the field or buried, and whether the scariest field is deferred until after value/commitment. Pairs with Baymard-style step drop-off framing.

teardownTargets.product: A SaaS free-trial → paid upgrade / cancellation flow (e.g. a tool with a trial-end paywall and a hard-to-find cancel path)
teardownTargets.why: Where honest persuasion vs. sludge is most visible: is the upgrade prompt a real value moment or confirmshaming, and does cancellation pass the FTC/regret test or is it a roach-motel dark pattern? Directly demonstrates the honest-Cialdini vs. dark-pattern line.

subNodes.label: Ambiguity aversion (Ellsberg, not just loss aversion)
subNodes.oneLiner: People reject a bet not because the odds are bad but because the odds are unknown; missing information is itself a cost.
subNodes.body: This is the single most underused model for AI/crypto. A user sending crypto or approving an AI action isn't loss-averse about a known downside, they're paralyzed by an UNKNOWN downside ('what will this contract actually do?', 'what will the agent actually touch?'). The fix is never 'reassure', it's 'convert ambiguity into risk' by naming the exact outcome, scope, and worst case. Ambiguity attitude is empirically distinct from risk attitude and not strongly correlated with it, so you must design for it separately.

subNodes.label: Loss aversion is real but context-dependent, λ≈1.0-1.5 not 2.25
subNodes.oneLiner: Losses loom larger than gains, but the famous '2x' coefficient came from 25 grad students and collapses toward ~1 in many field settings.
subNodes.body: The belief-shift here is professional credibility: most designers cite λ=2.25 as a law. Gal & Rucker (2018) and Yechiam's meta-analyses show it's smaller and disappears for small everyday stakes. For Sam's product this means you can't lazily invoke 'people hate losses' to justify scarcity timers; loss framing only bites when the loss is concrete, owned, and high-stakes (an on-chain irreversible transfer qualifies; a $9 SaaS trial mostly doesn't).

subNodes.label: System 1 / System 2 as a routing problem, not a personality
subNodes.oneLiner: The same user is fast-and-intuitive on low-stakes screens and slow-and-effortful at the money moment; design must switch registers at the switch point.
subNodes.body: Kahneman's real product lesson is not 'appeal to System 1'. It's: at a high-stakes irreversible step you WANT to kick the user into System 2 (a deliberate pause, a re-read, a typed confirmation), and everywhere else you want to stay out of their way. Confirmations that are frictionless everywhere (blind-signing) are the failure; confirmations that add friction on trivial steps are the other failure.

subNodes.label: Fogg Behavior Model B=MAP (motivation is the weakest lever)
subNodes.oneLiner: Behavior fires only when Motivation, Ability, and a Prompt coincide; ability and prompt are engineerable, motivation is not.
subNodes.body: When a crypto/AI flow leaks users, teams reach for motivation (bigger CTA, hype copy). Fogg's insight inverts this: at the money moment motivation is already maxed and the blocker is ability (cognitive/technical cost of understanding what you're approving) or a mistimed prompt. Reduce the ability cost (decode the transaction, pre-fill, chunk the form) before you touch persuasion.

subNodes.label: Reversibility as the master variable for how much friction to add
subNodes.oneLiner: Match the weight of the confirmation to the reversibility and blast radius of the action, not to a global 'reduce friction' rule.
subNodes.body: This is the systems-designer's edge and it unifies crypto + AI agents. The Tiered Controllability framework (map oversight to task risk × reversibility × autonomy scope) says: reversible action → one tap; irreversible on-chain transfer or an AI agent deleting/spending → force System 2. Most 'trust' failures are a reversibility/friction mismatch: irreversible actions treated as casual.

subNodes.label: Operational transparency & the labor illusion (friction can BUILD trust)
subNodes.oneLiner: Buell & Norton: showing the work being done raises perceived value and trust, sometimes even when it slows the result.
subNodes.body: Directly contradicts 'faster = better'. For AI especially, an agent that visibly reasons/checks ('scanning 3 sources... verifying contract... checking your balance') is trusted more than an instant black-box answer. This is the honest counter to fake spinners: real operational transparency at the moment of hesitation converts ambiguity into visible, legible process.

subNodes.label: Trust calibration / appropriate reliance (not maximal trust)
subNodes.oneLiner: The goal for AI actions is calibrated trust, matching user confidence to actual system reliability, not maximizing confidence.
subNodes.body: Over-reliance (automation bias) and under-reliance are BOTH failure modes and the most common one in deployed agents. A product that makes users trust it maximally is fragile; the durable design surfaces uncertainty and gives a real intervention point. This reframes 'reduce hesitation' as 'reduce MIScalibrated hesitation', which is what earns founder trust.

subNodes.label: Privacy calculus (disclosure is a running cost-benefit ledger)
subNodes.oneLiner: Users disclose sensitive data only when perceived benefit exceeds perceived privacy risk at that moment; each field re-runs the calculation.
subNodes.body: Explains fintech/crypto signup leak field-by-field: an SSN or seed-phrase-adjacent request spikes perceived risk and the ledger goes negative mid-form. The fix is local (justify the ask exactly where it's made, show the benefit inline, defer the scary field) not global reassurance in a footer.

subNodes.label: WYSIWYS / clear signing (decode intent at the confirmation)
subNodes.oneLiner: Any irreversible or high-blast-radius confirmation: sending crypto, approving a token allowance, an AI agent about to spend/send/delete. Replace machine-readable or vague strings ('Contract Interaction') with a human-readable statement of exactly what will happen, to whom, and the worst case.
subNodes.body: Example: Ethereum's ERC-7730 Clear Signing standard renders 'Approve unlimited USDC to 0x9a...' as 'This lets app X spend up to 50 USDC from your wallet'. Ledger/Trezor/MetaMask/WalletConnect back it. This is the canonical fix for ambiguity aversion.

subNodes.label: Bounded scope / spending caps as a first-class control
subNodes.oneLiner: When granting an agent or contract ongoing permission. Default the permission to the minimum viable scope and surface the cap as an editable number, not buried in advanced settings.
subNodes.body: Example: MetaMask custom spending caps: instead of 'unlimited approval', cap at the exact amount needed. For AI agents: 'this agent may spend up to $X / act only in these folders'. Converts open-ended ambiguity into a bounded, comprehensible risk.

subNodes.label: Deliberate System-2 speed bump at the point of no return
subNodes.oneLiner: Exactly at irreversible steps, and nowhere else. A typed confirmation, an address re-display, a 3-2-1 hold, or a plain-language 'you are about to X' summary that must be read.
subNodes.body: Example: Typing the recipient's last 4 characters, or 'type SEND to confirm'. Wise shows the exact recipient name + amount + fee on one final screen. The friction is the feature because it forces re-reading at the one moment re-reading matters.

subNodes.label: Progressive disclosure of sensitive fields (privacy-calculus staging)
subNodes.oneLiner: Long/high-anxiety signups (fintech, crypto KYC). Order fields by rising sensitivity, justify each scary ask inline, and defer the highest-risk field until after the user has invested and seen value.
subNodes.body: Example: Ask email/goal first (low risk, builds commitment), reveal SSN/ID upload last with a one-line 'why we need this + how it's stored' at the field, not in a footer.

subNodes.label: Commitment & consistency via a genuine small first yes
subNodes.oneLiner: When the eventual ask is large (fund a wallet, connect a bank, grant broad agent access). Start with a real, low-cost, reversible micro-commitment that the later step is consistent with.
subNodes.body: Example: 'Try one read-only query' before 'connect your account with write access'. Honest version: the small yes must be real value, not a manipulative foot-in-the-door that the user would fail Eyal's regret test on.

subNodes.label: Operational transparency during agent/AI work
subNodes.oneLiner: Any AI action with a perceptible wait or a black-box decision. Narrate the real steps and surface the actual sources/checks being run.
subNodes.body: Example: 'Reading your calendar... found 3 conflicts... drafting reply' with the specific items shown. Buell/Norton labor illusion, but honest: only show work that is actually happening.

subNodes.label: Anchor-and-default on the SAFE option
subNodes.oneLiner: Whenever a default exists at a risky choice. Make the reversible/safe/scoped option the pre-selected default and the anchor, since defaults dominate and most users never change them.
subNodes.body: Example: Default the token approval to 'this amount only' not 'unlimited'; default an AI agent to 'ask me before each action' not 'full autonomy', with autonomy as an explicit opt-in.

subNodes.label: Blind signing / opaque confirmation
subNodes.oneLiner: Presents accurate-but-unreadable data ('Contract Interaction', a raw hash) at the exact moment that is supposed to be the user's last line of defense. Triggers maximum ambiguity aversion, so users either abandon (leak) or click through blindly (the Bybit-class disaster). The confirmation exists but carries zero information.

subNodes.label: Global 'reduce friction' applied to irreversible steps
subNodes.oneLiner: One-tap-everything is correct for reversible actions and catastrophic for irreversible ones. Removing the System-2 speed bump at the point of no return maximizes conversion of the wrong action and destroys trust after the first bad transfer/agent action. Friction should be reversibility-weighted, not globally minimized.

subNodes.label: Fake progress / manufactured labor illusion
subNodes.oneLiner: A spinner that fabricates work the system isn't doing is the dark-pattern twin of honest operational transparency. It fails Eyal's regret test the moment users realize it, and in AI it teaches over-reliance on a system that's actually idle. Distinct from real transparency, which shows genuine steps.

subNodes.label: Drip pricing / late-revealed cost
subNodes.oneLiner: Baymard: 'extra cost too high/unexpected' is the #1 documented checkout-abandonment reason (~48%). Revealing fees (gas, spread, platform cut) only at the final step converts an anchored expectation into a felt loss precisely when the user is most committed, spiking loss-aversion-driven abandonment and distrust.

subNodes.label: Confirmshaming / manip-linked defaults on consent
subNodes.oneLiner: FTC 'Bringing Dark Patterns to Light' flags guilt-tripped opt-outs and pre-checked data-sharing that steer to maximum disclosure. Short-term it lifts a metric; it poisons the privacy-calculus ledger and fails the regret test, so it drives the 'reads as untrustworthy' perception Sam is trying to escape. Also increasingly illegal.

subNodes.label: Scarcity/urgency timers on low-stakes or fake losses
subNodes.oneLiner: Loss aversion is weak for small everyday stakes (λ near 1), so countdown timers on cheap or non-owned items are both ineffective AND read as manipulative to sophisticated users. Fabricated scarcity is a classic dark pattern; real, honest deadlines are fine, fake ones erode the trust they're meant to exploit.

subNodes.label: Motivation-first fixes for ability-limited flows
subNodes.oneLiner: Fogg: when users stall at a high-ability-cost step (understanding a transaction, a 14-field KYC form), teams add hype/bigger CTAs. Motivation is already high at the money moment; piling on motivation without cutting the ability cost just adds noise and the leak persists.

subNodes.label: Choice overload as a lazy explanation (or lazy 'just show fewer options')
subNodes.oneLiner: The jam study (Iyengar-Lepper 2000) does NOT robustly replicate: Scheibehenne et al. meta-analysis found average effect ≈ 0. Overload only bites under specific moderators (no prior preferences, high complexity, hard-to-compare options, time pressure). Cutting options blindly can lose sales; the real lever is decision-support (defaults, comparison, filtering), not fewer choices.

subNodes.label: The confirmation screen is technically 'correct' but semantically empt...
subNodes.oneLiner: The confirmation screen is technically 'correct' but semantically empty: the code renders the real payload (a hex calldata, a raw approval, an unlimited allowance) yet a code-reading designer sees that no decode/humanization layer exists between the RPC response and the DOM. The trust hole is an architecture gap, not a copy gap.

subNodes.label: Unlimited/open-ended approvals hidden behind friendly labels: the butt...
subNodes.oneLiner: Unlimited/open-ended approvals hidden behind friendly labels: the button says 'Approve' but the underlying call is `approve(spender, 2^256-1)`. Only someone reading the transaction data catches that the UI's cheerful microcopy is masking an unbounded permission grant.

subNodes.label: Client-side-only validation on the last-line-of-defense step: address/...
subNodes.oneLiner: Client-side-only validation on the last-line-of-defense step: address/amount checks that live in JS and can be bypassed or desynced from what's actually signed, so 'what the user sees' and 'what gets signed' diverge, the exact WYSIWYS failure.

subNodes.label: Optimistic UI that shows success before on-chain/settlement confirmati...
subNodes.oneLiner: Optimistic UI that shows success before on-chain/settlement confirmation: the code fires the success state on request-send, not on receipt. For irreversible money movement this manufactures false certainty and hides the real (ambiguous) pending state where the user's anxiety actually lives.

subNodes.label: Fee/gas/spread computed in a code path separate from the displayed pri...
subNodes.oneLiner: Fee/gas/spread computed in a code path separate from the displayed price, updating late or on a different render tick, which produces the drip-pricing 'the number jumped at the end' abandonment even when no one intended a dark pattern.

subNodes.label: AI agent 'confidence' shown as a UI flourish decoupled from any real u...
subNodes.oneLiner: AI agent 'confidence' shown as a UI flourish decoupled from any real uncertainty signal: a green check or a fixed 'high confidence' badge that isn't wired to model logprobs, tool-call success, or verification, so the interface asserts calibration it doesn't have, driving over-reliance.

subNodes.label: Autofilled/remembered sensitive values and broad default scopes set in...
subNodes.oneLiner: Autofilled/remembered sensitive values and broad default scopes set in state before the user consciously consents (pre-checked, pre-authorized), visible only by reading the initial state object, not the screen.

subNodes.label: Error and pending states that exist in the happy-path mockup but are u...
subNodes.oneLiner: Error and pending states that exist in the happy-path mockup but are unhandled in code: the hesitation moment (a stuck pending tx, a failed agent step, a timeout) renders as a frozen spinner or a raw stack trace, which is precisely where trust is won or lost and where design usually never looked because it never appears in Figma.

subNodes.label: Irreversibility not surfaced anywhere in the component tree: the app t...
subNodes.oneLiner: Irreversibility not surfaced anywhere in the component tree: the app treats a reversible edit and an irreversible transfer with the same generic confirm modal because there's no `reversible`/`riskTier` prop threading through, so the UI cannot possibly weight friction correctly.

topics.title: Methods & Teardown Strategy
topics.fullTitle: Research methods, UX metrics & teardown/critique strategy

methods.method: SUS (System Usability Scale), 10 items, scored 0-100
methods.measures: Perceived usability as a single benchmarkable number. Report with the Sauro-Lewis curved grade (68 = C = ~50th percentile; A range top-15%) against 500+ products, not the raw score. Use for pre/post redesign and cross-product teardown comparison.

methods.method: UMUX-Lite (2 items: usefulness + ease)
methods.measures: A near-substitute for SUS when you have no room for 10 items; Lewis et al.'s regression predicts SUS within ~1% of range. Ideal for embedding one micro-survey in a live product to track perceived quality continuously.

methods.method: Task-based usability metrics: completion rate, time-on-task, error count
methods.measures: Behavioral effectiveness/efficiency per task. Report completion rate with an adjusted-Wald confidence interval (not the naive Wald, which fails at small n) so you honestly bound 'X% of users can do this.'

methods.method: Switch/Timeline JTBD interviews (n≈6-12 recent adopters + churners)
methods.measures: The real job, the trigger event, and which of the four forces (push/pull/anxiety/habit) governs the switch. Recruit by recent behavior, reconstruct the timeline backward, tag emotional beats.

methods.method: Funnel analysis to a defined activation event
methods.measures: Step-level conversion; isolates the exact cliff. Requires clean event instrumentation - audit whether the activation event is even fired before trusting the funnel.

methods.method: Cohort retention curves (Amplitude/Mixpanel)
methods.measures: Whether the curve flattens (a retained core exists) or decays to zero (no job served). Segment by entry-behavior to find which first-action predicts retention - that action is your activation target.

methods.method: Trustworthy A/B testing with guardrails (Kohavi)
methods.measures: Causal effect of a change, IF you pre-register sample size, avoid peeking (or use sequential/always-valid methods), run an A/A test, check for Sample Ratio Mismatch, and run long enough to clear novelty/primacy effects.

methods.method: Heuristic evaluation (3-5 evaluators, Nielsen's 10) + severity 0-4
methods.measures: Expert-found usability violations with a ranked severity, catching ~60% of issues cheaply. The evaluator-diversity ('double experts' = domain + usability) raises hit rate.

methods.method: Cognitive walkthrough (Polson/Lewis 4 questions)
methods.measures: First-run learnability: at each step, will the user try the right action, see the control, associate it with their goal, and perceive progress? Best for onboarding leaks.

methods.method: DevTools/network + code read as an evaluation method
methods.measures: The mechanism behind a symptom: optimistic success states, swallowed errors, missing instrumentation, stale client state, latency of async ops. This is the differentiator - turning 'feels off' into a named root cause.

tactics: Lead every teardown with a leak-map: 3 ranked findings scored on frequency × impact × persistence, each tied to a Goal-Signal-Metric and a specific step. Ranking is what makes it credible and fee-worthy vs. a nitpick list.

Pair one attitudinal number with one behavioral number per claim (e.g., 'SUS 62 / D grade' + 'D7 retention 6%'), then expose the say/do gap. This is the fastest way to earn a data-literate founder's trust.

Reconstruct the anxiety force explicitly: for AI/crypto, name what the user is afraid of at each step (losing money, irreversibility, being scammed, looking dumb) and show which design element fails to lower it. Reframes 'bad UX' as 'unresolved anxiety' - your belief-shift thesis.

Read the code to convert symptom → mechanism → fix. 'The success toast lies because it fires on request-sent (see network tab), not on confirmation' is a sentence no screenshot-critic can write, and it's your signature.

Attack the instrumentation first: if the activation event isn't tracked, the founder literally cannot see their own leak. Recommending the missing event fire is high-leverage and immediately actionable.
Stress-test the founder's own metrics: check for peeking, SRM, novelty effect, and vanity aggregates. Debunking one bad number ('your win was a novelty spike') buys enormous credibility.

Use discount methods to FIND and quant methods to PROVE: 5-user walkthroughs to locate leaks, then a benchmark (SUS + task completion with CIs) to size them. Never confuse the two out loud - that discipline is itself a trust signal.

Publish teardowns in the belief-shift structure: counterintuitive claim → annotated evidence → named principle/heuristic → transferable rule. Target real AI/crypto products so 'Sam' recognizes his own product's disease.

Turn recommendations into testable hypotheses with a pre-declared success metric and required sample size, so the fix can be validated - this positions you as someone who ships measurable outcomes, not opinions.

resources.title: Quantifying the User Experience: Practical Statistics for User Research (2nd ed.)
resources.why: The canonical, defensible source for UX statistics: confidence intervals at small n, adjusted-Wald, sample-size math, and the SUS curved grading scale. This is the book that keeps your 'data' claims from being embarrassing.

resources.title: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing
resources.source: Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang & Ya Xu
resources.why: The definitive A/B testing text from the people who ran 20k+ experiments/yr at Microsoft/Google/LinkedIn. Peeking, SRM, novelty/primacy, Twyman's Law - exactly the traps founders fall into that you can debunk.

resources.title: Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications (HEART / Goals-Signals-Metrics)
resources.source: Kerry Rodden, Hilary Hutchinson, Xin Fu (Google, CHI 2010)
resources.why: Primary source for HEART and the Goals→Signals→Metrics discipline - the spine of any credible metrics recommendation in a teardown.

resources.title: 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design + How to Conduct a Heuristic Evaluation
resources.why: The 1994 canon (refined via factor analysis of 249 problems) plus NN/g's method guide with severity ratings. Your shared vocabulary for naming violations in a teardown.

resources.title: Demand-Side Sales 101 (and the Re-Wired Group's Switch/Forces of Progress method)
resources.why: Primary source for the Switch/Timeline interview and the four Forces of Progress - the interview technique that surfaces the 'anxiety' leak in AI/crypto adoption. Pair with the JTBD Radio archive.

resources.title: Rocket Surgery Made Easy (and Don't Make Me Think)
resources.why: The DIY qualitative usability-testing bible: how to moderate without leading or rescuing, how to write non-telegraphing tasks. Keeps your formative testing honest.

resources.title: MeasuringU (blog + tools)
resources.why: Ongoing primary source for the 'is 5 users enough' critique, SUS/UMUX-Lite benchmarks, sample-size-by-study-type, and CI calculators. The place to verify a statistical move before you publish it.

resources.title: Mastering Retention / product-analytics playbooks (funnels, cohorts, retention curves, North Star)
resources.why: Practical, current guidance on event instrumentation, activation events, cohorting, and reading the retention curve's flattening - the behavioral half of a teardown.

resources.title: How to do a Product Critique / How to choose the right UX metrics
resources.source: Julie Zhuo (The Looking Glass) & Kerry Rodden (GV Library)
resources.why: Zhuo's before/first-use/weeks-after critique structure and Rodden's metric-selection essay are the two best short reads on turning observation into a structured, credible critique.

resources.title: Growth.design case studies (annotated, principle-per-frame teardowns)
resources.why: The gold-standard format for a publishable teardown: annotated frames, one named psychology/heuristic principle each, ranked findings. Model your belief-shift posts on this structure, not the content.

resources.title: Observing the User Experience: A Practitioner's Guide to User Research
resources.why: Broad, rigorous coverage of the full research toolkit (interviews, diary studies, field, usability, surveys) with when-to-use guidance - the reference for matching method to question.

resources.title: Continuous Discovery Habits
resources.why: Turns JTBD/interviewing into a weekly, opportunity-solution-tree cadence founders can actually run - useful for positioning yourself as embedding research, not doing one-off audits.

teardownTargets.product: MetaMask (or Phantom) first-run: wallet creation + seed-phrase backup + first transaction sign
teardownTargets.why: 60-90% of crypto users churn before a first transaction; the seed-phrase and signing screens are the canonical anxiety + irreversibility + no-visibility-of-status leaks. Perfect cognitive-walkthrough + Forces-of-Progress case, and the network tab exposes optimistic 'submitted' states.

teardownTargets.product: A centralized exchange onboarding (Coinbase / Binance KYC + first deposit hold)
teardownTargets.why: KYC + a silent multi-day deposit hold is a classic invisible leak: the anxiety spike is the unexplained hold, not the form. Great for a Switch-interview-style teardown and a funnel/step-cliff analysis.

teardownTargets.product: An AI agent / long-generation tool (e.g., an autonomous coding or research agent, or an image generator)
teardownTargets.why: 10-90s async operations with weak system-status feedback, optimistic success toasts, and swallowed errors during tool-calls. Ideal for the read-the-code 'the success state lies' thesis and Nielsen H1 (visibility of system status).

teardownTargets.product: An LLM chat product's usage/limits + billing surface (context limits, token counters, plan gating)
teardownTargets.why: Copy that connects to no prior concept ('tokens', 'context window'), silent truncation, and unclear cost - a cognitive-walkthrough learnability leak plus a trust leak where the system hides its own state from the user.

teardownTargets.product: A vertical AI SaaS dashboard onboarding (e.g., an AI analytics or 'copilot' B2B tool's empty state → first value)
teardownTargets.why: Governance-first enterprise dashboards that demo well but leak at activation: the gap between 'connected data source' and 'got first insight.' Perfect for instrumentation-audit + cohort-retention + HEART Goals-Signals-Metrics, matching Ashutosh's core practice area.

subNodes.label: Demand-side JTBD (the Switch / Forces of Progress)
subNodes.oneLiner: People don't buy features, they hire a product to make progress in a struggling moment; the switch is a tug-of-war between Push + Pull (drive change) vs. Anxiety + Habit (resist it).
subNodes.body: For AI/crypto, the 'anxiety' force is the whole game. A powerful-but-untrusted product loses not because Pull is weak but because Anxiety (irreversibility, unclear cost, 'will I get scammed') and Habit outweigh it. Naming which force is losing tells you exactly what to fix, and it reframes churn from 'bad UX' to 'unresolved anxiety' - the belief-shift angle Sam will pay for.

subNodes.label: Goals → Signals → Metrics (HEART)
subNodes.oneLiner: Never pick a metric first; state the user goal, then the observable signal that proves it, then the number - so every metric traces back to a human outcome, not a dashboard vanity stat.
subNodes.body: AI/crypto dashboards drown founders in clickstream. HEART (Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task-success) plus the G-S-M discipline is how you argue 'this screen is leaking' with a metric that maps to a real goal, not 'DAU is down.' It's the spine of a credible teardown recommendation.

subNodes.label: The leak is a step, not a screen (funnel + retention curve reading)
subNodes.oneLiner: A product doesn't 'read as untrustworthy' in the abstract; a specific step has a conversion cliff, and a specific cohort's retention curve fails to flatten - find the cliff, then explain the mechanism.
subNodes.body: A flattening retention curve means you found a core group getting value; a curve that decays to zero means no real job is being served. For 'Sam,' locating the exact drop-off step (wallet-connect, first-transaction sign, API-key paste) converts vague 'users leak' into a fixable coordinate. This is the quantitative backbone under a teardown.

subNodes.label: Attitudinal vs. behavioral, and the say/do gap
subNodes.oneLiner: What users say (SUS, interviews, NPS) and what they do (funnels, session data) answer different questions; trust neither alone - triangulate.
subNodes.body: AI products demo well (high stated Happiness) but leak (low behavioral Retention). Catching that gap - great SUS, terrible D7 retention - is exactly the 'invisible problem' that separates a systems designer from a screenshot-critic.

subNodes.label: Trustworthiness of the measurement itself (Twyman's Law / SRM)
subNodes.oneLiner: Any metric or test result that looks too good or too surprising is probably wrong; before you believe a number, check the instrument (sample-ratio mismatch, peeking, novelty effect).
subNodes.body: Founders make product bets on broken experiments. A designer who can say 'your +12% lift is a Sample Ratio Mismatch artifact' or 'that's a novelty effect that will decay' earns founder trust instantly - it's the code-reader's skepticism applied to data.

subNodes.label: Severity = frequency × impact × persistence
subNodes.oneLiner: Rank every teardown finding on how often it hits, how bad it is when it does, and whether users can get past it - so you fix the load-bearing leak, not the loudest nitpick.
subNodes.body: Turns a teardown from a list of 40 gripes into 3 ranked, defensible priorities. Founders respect prioritization; a ranked leak-map is far more credible (and shareable) than an exhaustive complaint list.

subNodes.label: Discount / discovery vs. summative measurement
subNodes.oneLiner: Small-n qualitative testing (5 users) FINDS problems; it does NOT measure how many users have them - those are two different studies with two different sample sizes.
subNodes.body: The advanced move is knowing when '5 users' is a lie. For a benchmark or an A/B claim you need real n; for a formative teardown, 5 is fine. Conflating them is the most common credibility-killer in designer 'data' talk.

subNodes.label: Switch / Timeline interview (Moesta-Spiek)
subNodes.oneLiner: Before or alongside a teardown, to reconstruct the exact sequence from 'first thought' to 'first value' for real switchers/churners; interview people who recently adopted OR abandoned, walk their timeline backward, and tag each moment with which of the four forces was active.
subNodes.body: Example: Interviewing 8 people who abandoned a crypto exchange during KYC: the timeline reveals the 'anxiety' spike is not KYC itself but the unexplained 3-day hold on first deposit - a leak invisible in the UI screenshots.

subNodes.label: Heuristic evaluation with 3-5 evaluators + severity ratings
subNodes.oneLiner: Fast, cheap first pass on a product you're tearing down; each evaluator independently walks the flow against Nielsen's 10, logs violations, then you merge and rate severity 0-4.
subNodes.body: Example: 3 evaluators catch ~60% of the issues a full study would; you rate 'no visibility of system status during a 40s AI generation' as severity 4 because it drives task abandonment.

subNodes.label: Cognitive walkthrough for first-run / learnability
subNodes.oneLiner: When the leak is in onboarding or a novel flow (very common in AI/crypto) and the question is 'can a first-timer figure out the next action?' - step through each action asking the 4 Wharton/Polson questions (will they try to do it, notice the control, connect it to their goal, and see progress?).
subNodes.body: Example: Walk a non-crypto user through 'sign your first transaction': they never form the goal 'approve gas' because the word 'gas' connects to no prior concept - a pure learnability leak, not an aesthetic one.

subNodes.label: Read-the-code teardown (the signature edge)
subNodes.oneLiner: When the visible symptom (jank, false 'success' states, silent failures) hints at an implementation cause; open DevTools/network tab, read the event instrumentation, error handling, and state transitions to find the real mechanism.
subNodes.body: Example: A 'transaction submitted' toast fires on request-sent, not on-chain confirmation - reading the code shows the success state is optimistic and lies. That's a trust leak no visual critique would catch.

subNodes.label: SUS/UMUX-Lite benchmark with curved grade
subNodes.oneLiner: When you need a defensible single number to anchor a teardown or track a redesign; run SUS (10 items) or UMUX-Lite (2 items) and report the Sauro-Lewis percentile/letter grade, not the raw score.
subNodes.body: Example: 'This flow scores SUS 62 = grade C-/D, 35th percentile against 500+ products' lands harder with a founder than 'it feels clunky.'

subNodes.label: Funnel + cohort retention instrumentation audit
subNodes.oneLiner: When you have analytics access (or are recommending it); define the activation event, build the funnel to it, and split retention by cohort/entry-behavior to isolate which acquisition source or first-action predicts staying.
subNodes.body: Example: Cohorting by 'completed first AI generation in session 1' vs. not: the activated cohort retains 4x, proving the first-run is the leak, not pricing.

subNodes.label: Belief-shift teardown post structure
subNodes.oneLiner: When turning analysis into content; open with the counterintuitive claim ('This product's problem isn't the UI, it's that it lies about success'), show the annotated evidence, name the mechanism, then the fix and the general principle.
subNodes.body: Example: Growth.design-style annotated frames + a named psychological/heuristic principle per frame, ending with one transferable rule.

subNodes.label: '5 users is enough' applied to measurement
subNodes.oneLiner: Nielsen-Landauer's 1-(1-p)^n with p=.31 justifies 5 users for FINDING problems, not for quantifying rates or comparing designs. Nielsen used the z-distribution on tiny samples, inflating confidence (a stated ±24% is really ±32%). Using 5 users to claim 'Design B is better' or 'X% of users fail' is statistically indefensible and Sauro showed 8 is not enough for websites/consumer software.

subNodes.label: Peeking at an A/B test until it hits significance
subNodes.oneLiner: Continuously checking p-values and stopping at the first 'p<.05' inflates false positives 5-10x. Founders do this constantly. A designer who ships a redesign on a peeked result is building on noise - and a redesign 'win' that was a novelty/primacy effect will decay once users adapt.

subNodes.label: NPS / satisfaction survey as the health metric
subNodes.oneLiner: NPS is a single attitudinal number with huge variance and no diagnostic power; it tells you nothing about WHERE the leak is. Treating it as a product-quality KPI hides step-level behavioral failures and rewards demo-shine over retention.

subNodes.label: Vanity/aggregate metrics (DAU, total signups)
subNodes.oneLiner: They hide the cohort story. Signups can rise while activation rots. Without segmenting by cohort and mapping to a Goal-Signal-Metric, aggregates let a leaking product look healthy - the exact illusion founders fall for.

subNodes.label: Feature-list critique / redlining pixels
subNodes.oneLiner: Listing 40 spacing/contrast nits with no severity ranking and no mechanism reads as a junior audit. It doesn't tell the founder what to fix first or WHY users leave, so it doesn't build trust or justify a fee.

subNodes.label: Confirmation-driven usability test (leading tasks + moderator rescue)
subNodes.oneLiner: Writing tasks that telegraph the answer, or helping the user when they stall, manufactures success and buries the real leak. Krug's 'Rocket Surgery' point: the moderator's job is to shut up and observe, not to prove the design works.

subNodes.label: Solution-first JTBD interviews ('would you use a feature that...')
subNodes.oneLiner: Asking about hypothetical features gets you fiction. The Switch method demands you anchor on a real past purchase/abandonment and reconstruct the actual timeline and forces - hypotheticals produce agreeable lies, not demand insight.

subNodes.label: Optimistic/lying success states: a 'Success' toast fires on request-se...
subNodes.oneLiner: Optimistic/lying success states: a 'Success' toast fires on request-sent or client-side validation, not on server/on-chain confirmation. Reading the network tab reveals the UI asserts completion before the system knows - the single biggest trust leak in crypto and AI-agent products.

subNodes.label: Silent failure and swallowed errors: try/catch that logs nothing to th...
subNodes.oneLiner: Silent failure and swallowed errors: try/catch that logs nothing to the user, or a 200 response wrapping an application-level error. The user sees a spinner resolve to 'nothing happened' with no recovery path - invisible to a visual audit, obvious in the code.

subNodes.label: No visibility of system status during long async ops: AI generations a...
subNodes.oneLiner: No visibility of system status during long async ops: AI generations and blockchain confirmations take 10-90s with no progress signal, no elapsed time, no cancel. Violates Nielsen H1; users assume it hung and leave. The absence of a state is the bug.

subNodes.label: Irreversibility with no undo/confirmation gradient: signing a transact...
subNodes.oneLiner: Irreversibility with no undo/confirmation gradient: signing a transaction or a destructive AI action with a single click and no 'are you sure / here's exactly what happens' preview. Anxiety force spikes; the code shows there was never a confirmation step to design.

subNodes.label: Instrumentation gaps that make the leak unmeasurable: the key activati...
subNodes.oneLiner: Instrumentation gaps that make the leak unmeasurable: the key activation event isn't even tracked, so the funnel has a blind spot. A code-reading designer spots the missing event fire and can say 'you can't see your own leak because you never instrumented step 3.'

subNodes.label: Deceptive/optimistic loading (skeleton or fake progress bar that doesn...
subNodes.oneLiner: Deceptive/optimistic loading (skeleton or fake progress bar that doesn't reflect real state): reassures in demo but sets a false expectation that erodes trust when the real op fails behind it.

subNodes.label: Copy that connects to no prior concept ('gas', 'slippage', 'approve sp...
subNodes.oneLiner: Copy that connects to no prior concept ('gas', 'slippage', 'approve spender', 'context window', 'tokens'): a cognitive-walkthrough failure - the user can't form the goal because the label maps to nothing they know. Invisible to native crypto/AI designers who've lost their beginner eyes.

subNodes.label: Client-side state that desyncs from source of truth: balance/status ca...
subNodes.oneLiner: Client-side state that desyncs from source of truth: balance/status cached and not refetched, so the UI shows stale, contradictory numbers. Reads as 'the product is broken/untrustworthy' but is a state-management bug you only find by reading the data flow.
